body: To establish subsidy payment rates that ensure equal access, Lead Agencies must collect and analyze statistically valid and reliable data and have the option to conduct either a (1) market rate survey (MRS) reflecting variations in the price to parents of child care services by geographic area, type of provider, and age of child, or (2) an ACF pre-approved alternative methodology, such as a cost estimation model, which estimates the cost of care by incorporating both data and assumptions to estimate what expected costs would be incurred by child care providers and parents under different scenarios. All Lead Agencies must analyze the cost of providing child care through a narrow cost analysis or pre-approved alternative methodology. Prior to conducting the MRS or pre-approved alternative, Lead Agencies must consult with the State Advisory Council on Early Childhood Education and Care (designated or established pursuant to the Head Start Act (42 U.S.C. 9837b(b)(1)(A)(i)) or similar coordinating body, local child care program administrators, local child care resource and referral agencies, and other appropriate entities; and organizations representing child care caregivers, teachers, and directors. Prior to conducting the MRS or pre-approved alternative methodology, Lead Agencies must consult with the State Advisory Council on Early Childhood Education and Care (designated or established pursuant to the Head Start Act (42 U.S.C. 9837b(b)(1)(A)(i)) or similar coordinating body, local child care program administrators, local child care resource and referral agencies, and other appropriate entities; and organizations representing child care caregivers, teachers, and directors. Note: Any Lead Agency considering using an alternative methodology instead of a market rate survey to set payment rates, is required to submit a description of its proposed approach to OCC for pre-approval in advance of developing and conducting the alternative methodology. Advance approval is not required if the Lead Agency plans to implement both an MRS and an alternative methodology to set rates at a percentile of the market rate, but a Lead Agency conducting a limited market rate survey and using it to inform their cost model would need pre-approval for this approach. In its request for ACF pre-approval, a Lead Agency must provide details on the following elements of their proposed alternative methodology: • Overall approach and rationale for using proposed methodology • Description of stakeholder engagement • Data collection timeframe (if applicable) • Description of the data and assumptions included in the methodology, including how these elements will yield valid and reliable results from the model • Description of how the methodology will capture the universe of providers, and reflect variations by provider type, age of children, geographic location, and quality 4.2.1 Completion of the market rate survey or ACF pre-approved alternative methodology Did the Lead Agency conduct a statistically valid and reliable MRS or ACF pre-approved alternative methodology to meet the CCDF requirements to assess child care prices and/or costs and determine payment rates? Check only one based on which methodology was used to determine your payment rates. a. [x] Market rate survey. i. When were the data gathered (provide a date range; for instance, September – December 2023)? May 2024 b. [ ] ACF pre-approved alternative methodology. i. [ ] The alternative methodology was completed. ii. [ ] The alternative methodology is in process. If the alternative methodology was completed: When were the data gathered and when was the study completed? Describe any major differences between the pre-approved methodology and the final methodology used to inform payment rates. Include any major changes to stakeholder engagement, data, assumptions or proposed scenarios. If the alternative methodology is in progress: Provide a status on the alternative methodology and timeline (i.e., dates when the alternative methodology activities will be conducted, any completed steps to date, anticipated date of completion, and expected date new rates will be in effect using the alternative methodology). c. Consultation on data collection methodology. Describe when and how the Lead Agency engaged the following partners and how the consultation informed the development and execution of the MRS or alternative methodology, as appropriate. iii. State Advisory Council or similar coordinating body: In January 2024, the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) Advisory Panel members were notified that the Local Market Rate study was to begin that month. Panel members were encouraged to ask questions and review the state and federal requirements related to the MRS. Additionally, panel members were asked to provide input on any considerations to be made in the development and conduct of the study, as well as any guidance in rate setting. In April 2024, the ICCP Advisory Panel members were provided presentations on the process, status, and initial and results of the Market Rate Survey. Members were given the opportunity to review their previous recommendations, ask questions, and provide comments and feedback. iv. Local child care program administrators: In late Fall 2023, IDHW child care staff toured the state meeting on location with child care providers and hosting evening meetings for all child care providers and stakeholders in the following cities: Boise, Meridian, Caldwell, Coeur d’Alene, Idaho Falls, Pocatello, Twin Falls, Moscow, and Lewiston. At each meeting the Local Market Rate Survey was reviewed, data collection was discussed, and all attendees were encouraged to participate with the survey, ensure their information was accurate in RISE, and review the results of the survey. At each meeting time was dedicated to soliciting feedback on the market rates and ICCP payment practices. Additionally, child care administrators from the following locations are members of the ICCP Advisory Panel and received additional information and opportunities for feedback as described above: Boise, Rexburg, Nampa, Twin Falls, Pocatello, Coeur d'Alene, and Moscow. v. Local child care resource and referral agencies: Idaho's child care resource and referral offices are contractually required to gather, track, and report data specific to the Local Market Rate study. The statewide staff are actively involved in developing outreach and communication plans to collect current data from each provider. They contribute to the quality assurance procedures each year for collecting accurate and timely data for providers and conduct outreach when fixes are needed in data. vi. Organizations representing child care caregivers, teachers, and directors from all settings and serving all ages: In January 2024, the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) Advisory Panel members were notified that the Local Market Rate study was to begin that month. Panel members were encouraged to ask questions and review the state and federal requirements related to the MRS. Additionally, panel members were asked to provide input on any considerations to be made in the development and conduct of the study, as well as any guidance in rate setting. In April 2024, the ICCP Advisory Panel members were provided presentations on the process, status, and initial and results of the Market Rate Survey. Members were given the opportunity to review their previous recommendations, ask questions, and provide comments and feedback. Members of this group include leadership from the Idaho Association for the Education of Young Children, Idaho Voices for Children, Community Council of Idaho, the State Department of Education, the Idaho Infant Toddler Program, the Idaho Out-of-School Network, and the Idaho Head Start Association. vii. Other. Describe: NA d. An MRS must be statistically valid and reliable. An MRS can use administrative data, such as child care resource and referral data, if it is representative of the market. Please provide the following information about the market rate survey: i. When was the market rate survey completed? 6/28/2024 ii. What was the time period for collecting the information (e.g., all of the prices in the survey are collected within a three-month time period)? All known providers are asked to maintain rate data in the RISE database, facilities receive automated reminders to update their data quarterly, upon their login. Data used for the survey was downloaded May 2024. iii. Describe how it represented the child care market, including what types of providers were included in the survey: The providers included in the analysis were required to be active and located in the state of Idaho, and the type of care provided was limited to child care centers, group care, and family care. Both providers participating with ICCP and non-ICCP providers in all jurisdictions (licensed by cities) were included in the data system. iv. What databases are used in the survey? Are they from multiple sources, including licensing, resource and referral, and the subsidy program? The Market Rate data were provided by IdahoSTARS, the agency responsible for the state's Child Care Resource and Referral System. Statewide provider data for all state licensed and child care providers participating in the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) are maintained by IdahoSTARS using data from the RISE database. v. How does the survey use good data collection procedures, regardless of the method for collection (mail, telephone, or web-based survey)? The provider data required for the market rate analysis were retrieved from the RISE database and included basic provider information and full-time rates. Data provided in the study is collected every six months from all known providers to ensure accuracy and current rates for each providers in RISE. vi. What is the percent of licensed or regulated child care centers responding to the survey? 100.00 vii. What is the percent of licensed or regulated family child care homes responding to the survey? 100.00 viii. Describe if the survey conducted in any languages other than English: The Market Rate data were provided by IdahoSTARS, the agency responsible for the state's Child Care Resource and Referral System. Statewide provider data for all state licensed and child care providers participating in the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) are maintained by IdahoSTARS using data from the RISE database. The RISE database is available in Spanish. Additionally, non-English speaking providers are contacted by an interpreter to verify data. ix. Describe if data were analyzed in a manner to determine price of care per child: The RISE database allows for child care pricing to be entered in several modes, depending upon how the child care provider sets its prices. The modes are hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, and annually. Providers are encouraged to enter data for all of the modes they use. For example, one provider may have both a daily rate and a monthly rate that their customers can pay. Because there are multiple modes, and the providers are encouraged to use the modes that best suit them, child care rates are not standard among all providers. To provide an estimate of the market rate across the entire industry, one must either perform separate rate analyses by pricing mode or convert the pricing data to one consistent mode. In the interest of assessing the market rates for the entire population of providers at one time, the latter option was chosen. Based on information from the database, the two most common modes for rates are daily and monthly. To provide a single analysis for the entire industry, and to be consistent with Department of Health and Welfare’s (DHW) current policy to pay providers on a monthly basis, the monthly rate was chosen to be the basis for the market rate analysis. For converting the rates, the preference was to use monthly rates, followed in order by weekly rates, daily rates, and hourly rates. The multiplicative factors used to convert non -monthly rates to monthly rates were: • 4.28 weeks per month; • 21.4 days per month (5 days per week × 4.28 weeks per month); • 171.2 hours per month (40 hours per week × 4.28 weeks per month). x. Describe if data were analyzed from a sample of providers and if so, how the sample was weighted: No, all known licensed and subsidy participating child care providers are required to enter their information in to the provider data management system, RISE and their data was used in the rate calculations. e. Price variations reflected. The market rate survey data or ACF pre-approved alternative methodology data must reflect variations in child care prices or cost of child care services in specific categories. i. Describe how the market rate survey or pre-approved alternative methodology reflected variation in geographic area (e.g., county, region, urban, rural). Include information on whether parts of the State or Territory were not represented by respondents and include information on how prices or costs could be linked to local geographic areas. To evaluate the market structure, three geographic levels were examined (zip code, county, and region) as the basic unit for the analysis, and county was selected as the unit that best allowed differentiation between units without a large number of units with missing information. Some areas have higher overall rate structures than other areas due to differences in population density and differences in economic conditions. Following methodology used by several other states in their market rate analyses, principal components and cluster analyses were performed to divide counties into groups so that the counties within a group had similar rate structures while counties in different groups had differing rate structures. These analyses resulted in identifying three groups of counties. (2024 Idaho Child Care Market Rate Analysis). Using a single state-wide rate would not allow the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare to account for differences in rates due to geographic location, while using separate rates for each provider would be overly complex and would not account for similarities in rates within geographic regions. The process of determining a set of geographic regions for the market rate analysis required four steps: 1. Select the initial geographic units to use in the market rate structure analysis 2. Reduce the provider-level data to unit-level data 3. Determine the best measurements to use to compare and combine the units 4. Determine the best number of groups and to assign the geographic regions to the appropriate group. ii. Describe how the market rate survey or pre-approved alternative methodology reflected variation in type of provider (e.g., licensed providers, license-exempt providers, center-based providers, family child care home providers, home based providers). The Market Rate Analysis was restricted to three types of care: 1. Child care centers 2. Group care 3. Family (including relative) care. This is inclusive of all licensed child care providers and nearly all subsidy participating providers. Rates for in-home child care providers were excluded as the sample size was too small for reasonable rate setting. The decision was made to combine family and group care together for the market rate analysis with child care centers in a separate Market Rate Analysis. iii. Describe how the market rate survey or pre-approved alternative methodology reflected age of child (e.g., infant, toddler, preschool, school-age): With respect to age, children are divided into four categories in the IdahoSTARS database, these groups align with state licensing child to adult ratio requirements: 1. 0 - 23 months 2. 24 through 35 months 3. 36 through 59 months 4. 60 through 156 months. Within each of the age categories, rates are collected by IdahoSTARS for two "usage" categories: full-time and part-time. The Market Rate Structure Analysis incorporated these four categories and the market rate analysis provided percentiles for each of these four categories. iv. Describe any other key variations examined by the market rate survey or ACF pre- approved alternative methodology, such as quality level: NA 4.2.2 Cost analysis If a Lead Agency does not complete a cost-based pre-approved alternative methodology, they must analyze the cost of providing child care services through a narrow cost analysis. A narrow cost analysis is a study of what it costs providers to deliver child care at two or more levels of quality: (1) a base level of quality that meets health, safety, staffing, and quality requirements, and (2) one or more higher levels of quality as defined by the Lead Agency. The narrow cost analysis must estimate costs by levels of quality; include relevant variation by provider type, child’s age, or location; and analyze the gaps between estimated costs and payment rates to inform payment rate setting. Lead agencies are not required to complete a separate narrow cost analysis if their pre-approved alternative methodology addresses all of the components required in the narrow cost analysis. Describe how the Lead Agency analyzed the cost of child care through a narrow cost analysis or pre-approved alternative methodology for the FFY 2025–2027 CCDF Plan, including: a. How did the Lead Agency conduct a narrow cost analysis (e.g., a cost model, a cost study, existing data or data from the Provider Cost of Quality Calculator)? DHW utilized the data available in the RISE Database in order to obtain the provider wage data. By using the data from RISE, DHW was able to complete an analysis that represented all types of providers in all geographic regions of Idaho. The dataset was parsed by the type of care provided ( i.e. Center, Group, or Family) and by higher quality care by Idaho’s quality rating system. b. In the Lead Agency’s analysis, were there any relevant variations by geographic location, category of provider, or age of child? DHW utilized the data available in the RISE Database in order to obtain the provider wage data. By using the data from RISE, DHW was able to complete an analysis that represented all types of providers in all geographic regions of Idaho. The dataset was parsed by the type of care provided ( i.e. Center, Group, or Family) and by higher quality care by Idaho’s quality rating system. c. What assumptions and data did the Lead Agency use to determine the cost of care at the base level of quality (e.g., ratios, group size, staff compensations, staff training, etc.)? DHW utilized the data available in the RISE Database in order to obtain the provider wage data. By using the data from RISE, DHW was able to complete an analysis that represented all types of providers in all geographic regions of Idaho. The dataset was parsed by the type of care provided ( i.e. Center, Group, or Family) and by higher quality care by Idaho’s quality rating system. d. How does the Lead Agency define higher quality and what assumptions and data did the Lead Agency use to determine cost at higher levels of quality (e.g., ratio, group size, staffing levels, staff compensation, professional development requirements)? A Lead Agency can use a quality improvement system or other system of quality indicators (e.g., accreditation, pre-Kindergarten standards, Head Start Program Performance Standards, or State-defined quality measures). Idaho defines ￿higher quality￿ as any program participating with our Steps to Quality program in addition to any Head Start or nationally accredited facility. Steps to Quality participating providers meet a base level of quality focusing full implementation of enhanced health and safety practices in addition to enhanced professional development requirements for staff. Providers that deliver higher levels of quality verified at steps 3 through 6 implement additional quality practices related to lower adult to child ratios, ongoing professional development, staff qualifications, learning environment, curriculum and assessment use, and relationships amongst teachers and children. e. What is the gap between cost and price, and how did the Lead Agency consider this while setting payment rates? Did the Lead Agency target any rate increases where gaps were the largest or develop any long-term plans to increase rates based on this information? The estimated average cost to run a Center based facility was $343,598. The state of Idaho had an average reimbursement rate during that time of $72,480, which accounts for about 21% of their total costs. The estimated average costs to run a Group of Family based facility was $54,308. The state of Idaho had an average reimbursement rate of $26,640, which accounts for about 49% of their total costs. Idaho will continue to review data available in RISE to improve our understanding of the cost of providing child care in Idaho. Data collected will be used to inform all future rate updates as funding is available to insure that rates paid are sufficient to address the cost of providing care. 4.2.3 Publicly available report on the cost and price of child care The Lead Agency must prepare a detailed report containing the results of the MRS or ACF pre- approved alternative methodology and include the Narrow Cost Analysis if an ACF pre-approved alternative methodology was not conducted. The Lead Agency must make this report widely available no later than 30 days after completion of the report, including posting the results on the Lead Agency website. The Lead Agency must describe in the detailed report how the Lead Agency took into consideration the views and comments of the public or stakeholders prior to conducting the MRS or ACF pre-approved alternative methodology. a. Describe how the Lead Agency made the results of the market rate survey or ACF pre-approved alternative methodology report widely available to the public by responding to the questions below. i. Provide the date the report was completed: 8/6/2024 ii. Provide the date the report containing results was made widely available (no later than 30 days after the completion of the report): 8/20/2024 iii. Provide a link to the website where the report is posted and describe any other strategies the Lead Agency uses to make the detailed report widely available: https://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/providers/child-care-providers/child-care- resources iv. Describe how the Lead Agency considered partner views and comments in the detailed report. Responses should include which partners were engaged and how partner input influenced the market rate survey or alternative methodology: In late Fall 2023, IDHW child care staff toured the state meeting on location with child care providers and hosting evening meetings for all child care providers and stakeholders in the following cities: Boise, Meridian, Caldwell, Coeur d’Alene, Idaho Falls, Pocatello, Twin Falls, Moscow, and Lewiston. At each meeting the Local Market Rate Survey was reviewed, data collection was discussed, and all attendees were encouraged to participate with the survey, ensure their information was accurate in RISE, and review the results of the survey. At each meeting time was dedicated to soliciting feedback on the market rates and ICCP payment practices. Attendees at the local meetings included local child care program administrators, owners, and operators, child care staff, regional staff from the child care resource and referral agency, and organizations representing child care staff. In January 2024, the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) Advisory Panel members were notified that the Local Market Rate study was to begin that month. Panel members were encouraged to ask questions and review the state and federal requirements related to the MRS. Additionally, panel members were asked to provide input on any considerations to be made in the development and conduct of the study, as well as any guidance in rate setting. In April 2024, the ICCP Advisory Panel members were provided presentations on the process, status, and initial and results of the Market Rate Survey. Members were given the opportunity to review their previous recommendations, ask questions, and provide comments and feedback. Members discouraged the implementation of tiered reimbursements based on QRIS participation, and echoed the regional meeting attendees’ recommendation to set rates has high as the budget would allow to continue to improve subsidy participating children’s access to the full diversity of child care options. IDHW acknowledges and has met both of these recommendations.

body: The Lead Agency must set CCDF subsidy payment rates in accordance with the results of the current MRS or ACF pre-approved alternative methodology and at a level to ensure equal access for eligible families to child care services comparable with those provided to families not receiving CCDF assistance. Lead Agencies are also required to provide a summary of data and facts to demonstrate how payment rates ensure equal access, which means the Lead Agency must also consider the costs of base level care and higher quality care as part of its rate setting. Finally, the Lead Agency must re-evaluate its payment rates at least every 3 years. The ages and types of care listed in the base payment rate tables are meant to provide a snapshot of the categories of rates and are not intended to be comprehensive of all categories that might exist or to reflect the terms used by the Lead Agency for particular ages. If rates are not statewide, please provide all variations of payment rates when reporting base payment rates below. Base rates are the lowest, foundational rates before any differentials are added (e.g., for higher quality or other purposes) and must be sufficient to ensure that minimum health, safety, quality, and staffing requirements are covered. These are the rates that will be used to determine compliance with equal access requirements. 4.3.1 Payment rates a. To provide a single analysis for the entire industry, and to be consistent with Department of Health and Welfare’s (DHW) current policy to pay providers on a monthly basis, the monthly rate was chosen to be the basis for the market rate analysis. For converting the rates, the preference was to use monthly rates, followed in order by weekly rates, daily rates, and hourly rates. The preamble to the 2016 final rule states that a benchmark for adequate payment rates is the 75th percentile of the most recent MRS. The 75th percentile benchmark applies to the base rates. The 75th percentile is the number separating the lowest 75 percent of rates from the highest 25 percent. Setting rates at the 75th percentile, while not a requirement, would ensure that eligible families can afford three out of four child care providers. Describe: 4.3.3 Tiered rates, differential rates, and add-ons Lead Agencies may establish tiered rates, differential rates, or add-ons on top of their base rates as a way to increase payment rates for targeted needs (e.g., a higher rate for serving children with special needs). a. Does the Lead Agency provide any rate add-ons above the base rate? [ ] Yes. If yes, describe the add-ons, including what they are, who is eligible to receive the add-ons, and how often are they paid: [x] No. b. Has the Lead Agency chosen to implement tiered reimbursement or differential rates? [ ] Yes. [x] No. Tiered or differential rates are not implemented. If yes, identify below any tiered or differential rates, and, at a minimum, indicate the process and basis used for determining the tiered rates, including if the rates were based on the MRS or an ACF pre-approved alternative methodology. Check and describe all that apply: i. [ ] Differential rate for non-traditional hours. Describe: ii. [ ] Differential rate for children with special needs, as defined by the Lead Agency. Describe: iii. [ ] Differential rate for infants and toddlers. Note: Do not check if the Lead Agency has a different base rate for infants/toddlers with no separate bonus or add-on. Describe: iv. [ ] Differential rate for school-age programs. Note: Do not check if the Lead Agency has a different base rate for school-age children with no separate bonus or add-on. Describe: v. [ ] Differential rate for higher quality, as defined by the Lead Agency. Describe: vi. [ ] Other differential rates or tiered rates. For example, differential rates for geographic area or for type of provider. Describe: vii. If applicable, describe any additional add-on rates that you have besides those identified above. Does the Lead Agency reduce provider payments if the price the provider charges to private-pay families not participating in CCDF is below the Lead Agency’s established payment rate? [x] Yes. If yes, describe: Payment will be based on the lower of the provider’s usual and customary rates or the Local Market Rate (LMR) (IDAPA 16.06.12.502.01). [ ] No. 4.3.4 Establishing payment rates Describe how the Lead Agency established payment rates: a. What was the Lead Agency’s methodology or process for setting the rates or how did the Lead Agency use their data to set rates? Idaho has conducted a 2024 Market Rate Study, however due to budget constraints Idaho is not able to update our payment rates. Payment rates established using the 2021 rate study will be maintained until the next state fiscal year. At that time, the plan will be amended with the updated payment rates using the current study. Idaho continues to prioritize setting rates with the intention to fund the actual cost of childcare while maintaining program sustainability and subsidy access for children and families. b. How did the Lead Agency determine that the rates are adequate to meet health, safety, quality, and staffing requirements under CCDF? The updated market rate and resultant reimbursements focused on ensuring the ability of providers to meet the health, safety, and staffing requirements under the CCDF law. Child care providers rely on the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) for consistent, timely payments that sustain their businesses. Additionally, allowing the providers to bill ICCP in the same amount and methodology that they invoice their cash paying clients serves as a stable stream of income for their business. Current and future reimbursement rates were based on the actual charges reported by providers, regardless of their participation in ICCP. While receiving those reimbursement rates, providing participating in ICCP consistently demonstrated full compliance with health, safety, and supervision requirements. Additionally, ICCP funds the cost of health and safety inspections for all participating child care providers. c. How did the Lead Agency use the cost of care, either from the narrow cost analysis or the ACF pre-approved alternative methodology to inform rate setting, including how using the cost of care promotes the stabilization of child care providers? Rates are determined using Local Market Rate Survey, which is inclusive of all Idaho child care providers. Rates were gathered in real time and were inclusive of any rate increases charged by providers. After thorough review of the Local Market Rate Survey, rates are set with the intention to fund the actual cost of childcare while maintaining subsidy access for children and families. This encourages families to access a wide range of child care providers who participate in subsidies, limits out-of-pocket expenses for families, and maintains a sustainable program. Idaho has conducted a 2024 Market Rate Study, however due to budget constraints Idaho is not able to update our payment rates. Payment rates established using the 2021 rate study will be maintained until the next state fiscal year. At that time, the plan will be amended with the updated payment rates using the current study. d. How did the Lead Agency account for the cost of higher quality while setting payment rates? While Idaho's current QRIS participation rates are too small to provide statistically valid cost/quality comparisons, QRIS participation continues to improve, and we are piloting the use of the Cost of Quality Calculator with some QRIS participating programs to better understand their unique expenses. Additionally, when completing Idaho’s Local Market Rate Survey all programs considered to be high quality were included in the rate calculation. High quality facilities with rates high enough to be considered outliers were not excluded. The higher rates charged by those facilities were intentionally included to ensure that rates were statistically valid and inclusive of the higher cost of high quality child care. e. Identify and describe any additional facts (not covered in responses to 4.3.1 – 4.3.3) that the Lead Agency considered in determining its payment rates to ensure equal access. When defining policies for families and providers, we review both balancing continuity for children and policies that are fair to providers. The decision to allow additional rate above the required co-payment is a combination of both levers. Ensuring families have choice and access, while also allowing child care businesses to identify their costs as such to promote and provide quality care. Providers and advocacy groups continue to support the practice of allowing child care providers to charge above the Local Market Rate, as demonstrated in comments provided as feedback to this plan. Families participating with the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) continue to access every type of child care provider, including high quality providers participating in Idaho's QRIS program and NAEYC accreditation. Ongoing Market Rate updates continue to ensure that ICCP participating providers will maintain their participation with ICCP, and families will continue to be able to access Idaho's best child care choices.

body: Lead Agencies must use subsidy payment practices that reflect practices that are generally accepted in the private pay child care market. The Lead Agency must ensure timeliness of payment to child care providers by paying in advance or at the beginning of delivery of child care services. Lead Agencies must also support the fixed cost of child care services based on paying by the child’s authorized enrollment, or if impracticable, an alternative approach that will not undermine the stability of child care programs as justified and approved through this Plan. Lead Agencies must also (1) pay providers based on established part-time or full-time rates rather than paying for hours of service or smaller increments of time, and (2) pay for reasonable, mandatory registration fees that the provider charges to private-paying parents. These policies apply to all provider types unless the Lead Agency can demonstrate that in limited circumstances the policies would not be considered generally-accepted payment practices. In addition, Lead Agencies must ensure that child care providers receive payment for any services in accordance with a payment agreement or an authorization for services, ensure that child care providers receive prompt notice of changes to a family’s eligibility status that could impact payment, and have timely appeal and resolution processes for any payment inaccuracies and disputes. 4.4.1 Prospective and enrollment-based payment practices Lead Agencies must use payment practices for all CCDF child care providers that reflect generally- accepted payment practices of providers serving private-pay families, including paying providers in advance or at the beginning of the delivery of child care services and paying based on a child’s authorized enrollment or an alternative approach for which the Lead Agency must demonstrate paying for a child’s authorized enrollment is not practicable and it will not undermine the stability of child care programs. Lead Agencies may only use alternate approaches for subsets of provider types if they can demonstrate that prospective payments and authorized enrollment-based payment are not generally-accepted for a type of child care setting. Describe the Lead Agency payment practices for all CCDF child care providers: a. Does the Lead Agency pay all provider types prospectively (i.e., in advance of or at the beginning of the delivery of child care services)? [ ] Yes. If yes, describe: [x] No, it is not a generally-accepted payment practice for each provider type. If no, describe the provider type not paid prospectively and the data demonstrating it is not a generally-accepted payment practice for that provider type, and describe the Lead Agency’s payment practice that ensures timely payment for that provider type: Payments are issued directly to eligible providers via check or direct deposit on the second business day of the month following the month when care was provided. For example, payment for care provided in September would be made on the second business day of October. Idaho is developing a plan for prospective payments in alignment with the 2024 CCDF Rules. Idaho intends to apply for a transitional waiver while we work to implement prospective payments. b. Does the Lead Agency pay based on authorized enrollment for all provider types? [ ] Yes. The Lead Agency pays all providers by authorized enrollment and payment is not altered based on a child’s attendance or the number of absences a child has. [ ] No, it is not a generally-accepted practice for each provider type. If no, describe the provider types not paid by authorized enrollment, including the data showing it is not a generally-accepted payment practice for that provider type, and describe how the payment policy accounts for fixed costs: [x] It is impracticable. Describe provider type(s) for which it is impracticable, why it is impracticable, and the alternative approach the Lead Agency uses to delink provider payments from occasional absences, including evidence that the alternative approach will not undermine the stability of child care programs, and thereby accounts for fixed costs: Idaho requires that rates charged by the child care provider must not exceed the usual and customary rates charged for child care to persons not entitled to receive benefits under ICCP. If a child care provider's established rates are not altered based on a child's attendance the subsidy payment is not altered. Idaho intends to apply for a transitional waiver as we develop additional strategies to pay by authorized enrollment not linked to a child's number of absences. 4.4.2 Other payment practices Lead Agencies must (1) pay providers based on established part-time or full-time rates rather than paying for hours of service or smaller increments of time, and (2) pay for reasonable, mandatory registration fees that the provider charges to private-paying parents, unless the Lead Agency provides evidence that such practices are not generally-accepted for providers caring for children not participating in CCDF in its State or Territory. a. Does the Lead Agency pay all providers on a part-time or full-time basis (rather than paying for hours of service or smaller increments of time)? [x] Yes. [ ] No. If no, describe the policies or procedures that are different than paying on a part- time or full-time basis and the Lead Agency’s rationale for not paying on a part-time or full-time basis: b. Does the Lead Agency pay for reasonable mandatory registration fees that the provider charges to private-paying parents? [x] Yes. If yes, identify the fees the Lead Agency pays for: One-time fees for registering a child in a child care facility are payable above the local market rate if the fee is charged to all who enroll in the facility. Reimbursement cannot exceed $250 and must be usual and customary rates charged to all families. Registration fees are separate from local market rates. ( IDAPA 16.06.12.500.02). [ ] No. If no, identify the data and how data were collected to show that paying for fees is not a generally-accepted payment practice: c. Describe how the Lead Agency ensures that providers are paid in accordance with a written payment agreement or an authorization for services that includes, at a minimum, information regarding provider payment policies, including rates, schedules, any fees charged to providers, and the dispute-resolution process: All Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) child care providers sign an 'ICCP Provider Agreement' annually which describes the provider's and the State's requirements and responsibilities while participating in the Idaho Child Care Program. Additionally, all new providers complete a subsidy orientation with an IdahoSTARS Resource Specialist to review the participation requirements billing practices for ICCP. The ICCP Provider Agreement and the orientation both reference Child Care IDAPA and ensure providers know, read and understand the rights and responsibilities, which include the dispute resolution process as identified as 'PROVIDER NOTIFICATION' in IDAPA 16.06.12.752. The ICCP Provider Agreement also reminds providers that they are subject to, and protected by, the entire chapter of IDAPA 16.06.12 "Rules Governing the Idaho ChildCare Program (ICCP)". This chapter explains payment policies (16.06.12.500.-505), and the dispute-resolution process (16.06.12.003 and 16.06.12.752). d. Describe how the Lead Agency provides prompt notice to providers regarding any changes to the family’s eligibility status that could impact payments, and such a notice is sent no later than the day that the Lead Agency becomes aware that such a change will occur: Providers are notified of projected payment as soon as the client's eligibility is determined, if a family's projected payment amount changes, if the case closes, or requires the completion of a reevaluation to remain eligible. Providers receive a monthly statement of all issued payments with the payment. e. Describe the Lead Agency’s timely appeal and resolution process for payment inaccuracies and disputes: Administrative Appeals - ( IDAPA 16.06.12.003) All administrative appeals are governed by provisions of IDAPA 16.05.03, "Rules Governing Contested Cases Proceedings and Declaratory Rulings." Clients have 30 days from the date of a decision to request a fair hearing. Fair hearing officers review and responds to all requests within five calendar days of the "Fair Hearing Requested" task being set. They communicate the status of reinstatement/continuance of benefits pending the hearing result to the customer within five calendar days of the "Fair Hearing Requested" task being set, then work with the client to coordinate and manage all aspects of a fair hearing to completion. (Benefits Process Manual: "Fair Hearing Process"). Provider Notification - ( IDAPA 16.06.12.752) "When the Department determines actions defined in Sections 701 through 705, 750,and 751 [Overpayment, Intentional Program Violation, Denial of Payment, Funding Restrictions, Termination of Provider Status, Refusal to Enter Into An Agreement] of these rules are appropriate, it will send written notice of the decision to the provider or person. The notice will state the basis for the action, the length of the action, the effect of the action on that person's ability to provide services under state and federal programs, and the person's appeal rights." f. Other. Describe any other payment practices established by the Lead Agency: 4.4.3 Payment practices and parent choice How do the Lead Agency’s payment practices facilitate provider participation in all categories of care? Providers and advocacy groups continue to support the practice of allowing child care providers to charge above the Local Market Rate, as demonstrated in feedback provided for this plan. This policy encourages and maintains a majority of Idaho’s child care providers’ voluntary participation with the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP). Idaho’s payments are timely, and providers receive accurate payment information each month. Providers have quick and easy access to DHW staff via email, phone call, or in-office visit to assist with any payment questions or issues. Families participating in ICCP continue to access every type of child care provider, including high quality providers participating in Idaho's QRIS program and NAEYC accreditation. More than 10% of all children participating in child care subsidy in Idaho are being served in programs considered to be high quality as defined in Idaho’s Quality Ratings and Improvement System. Ongoing Market Rate updates continue to ensure that providers participating in ICCP will maintain their participation with ICCP, and families will continue to be able to access Idaho's best child care choices.

body: Building a supply of high-quality child care that meets the needs and preferences of parents participating in CCDF is necessary to meet CCDF’s core purposes. Lead Agencies must support parent choice by providing some portion of direct services via grants or contracts, including at a minimum for children in underserved geographic areas, infants and toddlers, and children with disabilities. 4.5.1 Child care services available through grants or contracts Does the Lead Agency provide direct child care services through grants or contracts for child care slots? [ ] Yes, statewide. Describe how the Lead Agency ensures that parents who enroll with a provider who has a grant or contract have choices when selecting a provider: [ ] Yes, in some jurisdictions, but not statewide. Describe how many jurisdictions use grants or contracts for child care slots and how the Lead Agency ensures that parents who enroll with a provider who has a grant or contract have choices when selecting a provider: [x] No. If no, describe any Lead Agency plans to provide direct child care services through grants and contracts for child care slots: Currently, IDHW does not pay direct child care services through grants and contracts through child care slots. IDHW will request a waiver to obtain technical assistance on how to implement this requirement. If no, skip to question 4.5.2. i. If yes, identify the populations of children served through grants or contracts for child care slots (check all that apply). For each population selected, identify the number of slots allocated through grants or contracts for direct service of children receiving CCDF. [ ] Children with disabilities. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: [ ] Infants and toddlers. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: [ ] Children in underserved geographic areas. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: [ ] Children needing non-traditional hour care. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: [ ] School-age children. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: [ ] Children experiencing homelessness. Number of slots allocated through grants or contracts: [ ] Children in urban areas. Percent of CCDF children served in an average month: [ ] Children in rural areas. Percent of CCDF children served in an average month: [ ] Other populations. If checked, describe: ii. If yes, how are rates for slots funded by grants and contracts determined by the Lead Agency? 4.5.2 Care in the child’s home (in-home care) The Lead Agency must allow for in-home care (i.e., care provided in the child’s own home) but may limit its use. Will the Lead Agency limit the use of in-home care in any way? [x] Yes. [ ] No. If yes, what limits will the Lead Agency set on the use of in-home care? Check all that apply. i. [x] Restricted based on the minimum number of children in the care of the in- home provider to meet the Fair Labor Standards Act (minimum wage) requirements. Describe: The Department limits the approval of all in-home child care under ICCP to the following circumstances: There are three (3) or more ICCP eligible children in the home who are not in school at any time during the day and require child care. (16.06.06.12.400.01) Parents are responsible to pay persons providing care in the child’s home the minimum wage, as required by the Fair Labor Standards Act (29 U.S.C. 206a) and other applicable state and federal requirements. (IDAPA 16.06.12.502.03) ii. [x] Restricted based on the in-home provider meeting a minimum age requirement. Describe: Age of Provider - (IDAPA 16.06.12.0802.01) All child care providers providing services must be 18 years old or older. Persons sixteen or seventeen years old may provide child care if they have direct, on-site supervision from a licensed child care provider who is at least 18 years old. iii. [x] Restricted based on the hours of care (i.e., certain number of hours, non- traditional work hours). Describe: Requirements for In-Home Care Under ICCP - (IDAPA 16.06.12.400.02.a and b) Parents must contact the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (DHW) to request approval of in-home child care. Only parents who have qualified activities outside their home will be considered for in-home care approval. DHW limits the approval of all in-home child care under ICCP for fewer than three children in the home. If there are fewer than three children in the home who are eligible for ICCP and require child care, in-home care will be approved by DHW only when one of the following special circumstances are met: 1. Parents' qualifying activity occurs during times when out-of-home care is not available. If child care is needed during any period when out-of-home care is not available, in-home care will be approved for the entire time care is needed. A family is not expected to change between out-of-home and in-home care 2. The family lives in an area where out-of-home care is not available. iv. [ ] Restricted to care by relatives. (A relative provider must be at least 18 years of age based on the definition of eligible child care provider.) Describe: v. [x] Restricted to care for children with special needs or a medical condition. Describe: Requirements for In-Home Care Under ICCP - (IDAPA 16.06.12.400.02.c) Parents must contact the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (DHW)to request approval of in-home child care. Only parents who have qualified activities outside their home will be considered for in-home care approval. DHW limits the approval of all in-home child care under ICCP to fewer than three children in the home. If there are fewer than three children in the home who are eligible for ICCP and require child care, in-home care will be approved by DHW only a child has a verified illness or disability that would place the child or other children in an out-of-home facility at risk. vi. [ ] Restricted to in-home providers that meet additional health and safety requirements beyond those required by CCDF. Describe: vii. [ ] Other. Describe: 4.5.3 Shortages in the supply of child care Lead Agencies must identify shortages in the supply of child care providers that meet parents’ needs and preferences. What child care shortages has the Lead Agency identified in the State or Territory, and what is the plan to address the child care shortages? a. In infant and toddler programs: i. Data sources used to identify shortages: Facility data, including age ranges of children served and slots available, is collected in the RISE Application with regular reminders to facility administrators to update data. Data is also collected on the direct referrals to IdahoSTARS for infant and toddler care. For quality efforts, IdahoSTARS is expanding Infant Mental Health Endorsement for Infant Educators, tracking progress through endorsement and number of Infant Educators endorsed in the state. Pyramid Model implementation with programs and providers serving children birth to three years of age includes data collection on the programs’ Benchmarks of Quality, results of fall and spring Teaching Pyramid Infant-Toddler Observation Scales (TPITOS), and two mid-year surveys examining impact and participant experience through implementation of the Pyramid Model practices. IdahoSTARS collects and analyzes specific data related to childcare availability, including information on programs that have opened or closed. When a program closes, IdahoSTARS assists families in finding alternative childcare that meets their needs, if available, through referrals and follow-up surveys to ensure they were able to secure care. While IdahoSTARS’ primary role is increasing access to high- quality child care, project activities do support broader understanding of infant toddler shortages such as data collection and reporting, along with professional development offerings that can influence availability and sustainability of infant and toddler care. Childcare programs report their capacity and waitlist information in the RISE system, which is used in referrals to help families locate available childcare. This data also allows IdahoSTARS to identify gaps in care, particularly for infant and toddler care. Current data indicates that there is a shortage of infant and toddler care, as families often report difficulty in finding suitable care for these age groups. ii. Method of tracking progress: Facility data is entered directly into the RISE application by program administrators. Referral data is entered into RISE by IdahoSTARS Resource Specialists. Quality improvement and professional development data is housed in RISE and within secure project management and survey software. iii. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using family child care homes In collaboration with statewide partners, IdahoSTARS provides supports to those interested in starting a child care business helping to ensure their successful start- up. In addition, quality support with aligned grants are available to new programs. IdahoSTARS also provides additional program incentives to family child care homes expanding their support and engagement in quality improvement activities The specific data elements that identify infant and toddler care shortages include waitlists, reported openings/closures, and families who report being unable to find care through referrals. These indicators point to existing shortages in the availability of infant and toddler care. Additionally, Business Practice Cohorts help child care providers stay in business by offering modules on budgeting, record-keeping, and marketing. IdahoSTARS also supports home providers by encouraging them to become ICCP certified and assists them in expanding their childcare businesses. iv. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using child care centers? In collaboration with statewide partners, IdahoSTARS provides supports to those interested in starting a child care business helping to ensure their successful start- up. In addition, quality support with aligned grants are available to new programs. IdahoSTARS also provides additional program incentives to child care centers expanding their support and engagement in quality improvement activities. Implementing the Pyramid Model in childcare settings can improve the quality of care provided to infants and toddlers by equipping caregivers with strategies to support the social-emotional development of young children. By enhancing caregivers' skills, the model helps create more stable and supportive environments, making these settings more attractive for both caregivers and parents, potentially reducing shortages. Integrating ITMH principles into childcare practices ensures that caregivers are trained to recognize and support the mental health needs of infants and toddlers. This training can lead to higher-quality care, better child outcomes, and increased job satisfaction among caregivers, which could help retain staff and reduce shortages. In the context of infant-toddler care shortages, direct referrals can help ensure that available spots in quality programs are filled efficiently, reducing the gap between supply and demand. Additionally, referrals to specialized programs or training can support caregivers in developing the skills needed for infant-toddler care, potentially increasing the number of providers willing and able to care for this age group. By improving business practices, childcare providers can create more sustainable operations. For example, better financial management might allow a provider to offer competitive wages or benefits, which could attract and retain caregivers for infant-toddler care. Additionally, efficient staffing practices can ensure that more spots are available for infants and toddlers, helping to alleviate shortages. b. In different regions of the State or Territory: i. Data sources used to identify shortages: Facility data, including age ranges of children served, slots available, and program location is collected in the RISE Application with regular reminders to facility administrators to update data. Data is also collected on the direct referrals by region to IdahoSTARS for child care. ii. Method of tracking progress: IdahoSTARS sets quality improvement targets which are regularly reviewed for recruitment and retention of programs into the state quality rating and improvement system and the Idaho Child Care Program. Strategic progress is tracked and reported to the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. iii. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using family child care homes? IdahoSTARS will continue to incentivize family child care homes for their engagement in quality initiatives, and will continue to provide technical assistance to new child care programs along with opportunities to receive start-up grant funding. The efforts described by IdahoSTARS address child care supply in different regions by focusing on a few key strategies: Incentivizing Family Child Care Homes: By providing incentives for family child care homes to engage in quality initiatives, IdahoSTARS is encouraging existing child care providers to improve and maintain high standards. This can lead to more reliable and quality child care options across various regions, as providers are motivated to meet these higher standards. Technical Assistance to New Child Care Programs: Offering technical assistance to new child care programs is crucial for increasing the supply of child care in underserved or growing regions. By helping new providers navigate the complexities of starting a child care business, IdahoSTARS ensures that these programs are more likely to succeed and sustain their operations, thereby increasing the overall availability and sustainability of child care. Start-Up Grant Funding: Providing opportunities for start-up grant funding helps reduce the financial barriers to opening new child care facilities. This is particularly important in regions where child care supply is low, as it makes it easier for new providers to enter the market and serve communities that may lack sufficient child care options. iv. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using child care centers? IdahoSTARS will continue to incentivize child care centers for their engagement in quality initiatives, and will continue to provide technical assistance to new child care programs along with opportunities to receive start-up grant funding. The efforts mentioned focus on addressing regional shortages in child care by identifying and responding to gaps in child care availability and supporting child care providers in those areas. Here's how the efforts are structured to focus on regional shortages: Identifying Shortages: IdahoSTARS uses data from waitlists, reported openings/closures, and feedback from families who were unable to find care to identify regions across the state where there are significant shortages in child care, particularly in child care centers. Incentivizing Quality: IdahoSTARS incentivizes family child care homes to engage in quality initiatives, which can improve the overall availability and quality of care in regions where shortages are identified. Supporting New Programs: IdahoSTARS provides technical assistance and start-up grant funding to help establish new child care programs in regions with shortages. This directly addresses the lack of available child care by encouraging the development of new providers. Sustaining Existing Providers: Through Business Practice Cohorts, IdahoSTARS offers targeted support to help existing child care centers stay in business, especially in areas where child care options are limited. These cohorts cover essential business skills like budgeting, record keeping, staffing, and marketing, which are critical for the sustainability of these centers. Encouraging ICCP Certification: By encouraging center directors and owners who do not currently accept Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) subsidies to become certified, IdahoSTARS aims to increase the availability of subsidized child care in regions where there are shortages, making care more accessible to low-income families. c. In care for special populations: i. Data sources used to identify shortages: Data is collected by IdahoSTARS on direct ￿enhanced￿ referrals, those that necessitate additional support and follow up due to special child and family needs. ii. Method of tracking progress: Data is collected in the RISE Application by Resource Specialists on enhanced referral. iii. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using family child care homes? IdahoSTARS is expanding their quality efforts to increase the availability of quality programs better able to meet the diverse needs of young children through implementation of the Pyramid Model. For enhanced referrals, the Child Care Resource Center staff, including Child Care Health Consultants, will be available to support successful access and inclusion of children with disabilities into child care settings. iv. What is the plan to address the child care shortages using child care centers? IdahoSTARS is expanding their quality efforts to increase the availability of quality programs better able to meet the diverse needs of young children through implementation of the Pyramid Model. For enhanced referrals, the Child Care Resource Center staff, including Child Care Health Consultants, will be available to support successful access and inclusion of children with disabilities into child care settings. 4.5.4 Strategies to increase the supply of and improve quality of child care Lead Agencies must develop and implement strategies to increase the supply of and improve the quality of child care services. These strategies must address child care in underserved geographic areas; infants and toddlers; children with disabilities, as defined by the Lead Agency; and children who receive care during non-traditional hours. How does the Lead Agency identify any gaps in the supply and quality of child care services and what strategies are used to address those gaps for: a. Underserved geographic areas. Describe: According to the Idaho Needs Assessment completed in April 2024 by the Idaho School Readiness Project (with funding from the Preschool Development Birth-5 grant), Idaho's supply of child care is especially difficult to measure: "The potential demand for early childhood care and education (ECCE) in Idaho based on American Community Survey (ACS) data on the count and percentage of children ages birth through 5 with all parents in the labor force and, therefore, potentially needing care. To estimate the availability of ECCE relative to the potential demand, researchers employ a variety of methodologies to identify ￿child care deserts￿ where the quantity of ECCE slots does not meet the potential demand for care. 10 For all methodologies, it is necessary to have reliable early care licensed capacity data to compare with the counts of young children potentially needing care. As indicated above, it is only possible to provide broad-range estimates of licensed capacity for Idaho child care, and these estimates are only possible for children ages birth through 12. Therefore, it is not possible, with currently available data, to accurately assess the adequacy of ECCE capacity in the state." (Idaho Needs Assessment Report page 47) The report also notes: "A basic methodology for determining child care deserts is calculating the gap between licensed slots and the number of children with all parents in the labor force (as a proxy for the number of children potentially needing care). The Center for American Progress definition is more nuanced: ￿A child care desert is any census tract with more than 50 children under age 5 that contains either no child care providers or so few options that there are more than three times as many children as licensed child care slots.￿ In their 2017 study, they estimated that 49% of people in Idaho lived in a child care desert. This was similar to the national rate of 50%." (Idaho Needs Assessment Report page 47) With the outcome of this most recent report unable to provide specificity related to underserved geographic areas, Idaho will continue to refine data collection efforts utilizing technical assistance and partners to continue our research in this area. With an understanding that nearly half the state lacks adequate access to needed child care, Idaho continues to have regionally located child care consultants available to provide on-site and over-the-phone technical assistance to new and existing providers considering providing child care in underserved geographic areas. Consultants have knowledge and resources available to assist providers serving children in rural and remote communities, as well as in the start-up and expansion of child care businesses. Start up grants are available to newly enrolled child care providers. The grant is a reimbursement grant that may cover such expenses as background checks for the provider or items needed to pass their health inspection. b. Infants and toddlers. Describe: IdahoSTARS delivers professional development specific to infants and toddlers. In addition, IdahoSTARS provides supports and funding for Infant Mental Health Endorsement, to include reflective consultation and other provider retention activities. Based on data analysis from our RISE application, we have identified a significant shortage of infant and toddler care providers. Our findings indicate that many infant and toddler teachers frequently transition to preschool positions or leave the field altogether. In response to this issue, we have recognized the need for targeted professional development tailored specifically to the unique needs and challenges of infant and toddler care. The Infant Mental Health endorsement addresses this need by formally recognizing providers' expertise in this specialized area, thereby enhancing their marketability. Additionally, the endorsement supports reflective practice as a retention strategy, offering ongoing support to caregivers to address challenges and improve their practice. c. Children with disabilities. Describe: IdahoSTARS is working with state partners to expand access to child care slots for children with disabilities through enhanced referrals, collaborative developmental screening activities, through professional development on specific disabilities and inclusive practices, and through implementation of the Pyramid Model and aligned behavioral supports. The gap in access to child care slots for children with disabilities can be identified through a series of data collection, analysis, and stakeholder engagement activities, particularly focusing on the following areas: Enhanced Referrals: Data Collection: Identify the current number and types of referrals made for children with disabilities to child care providers. This includes understanding the rate of successful placements versus referrals that do not result in placement. Gap Identification: A gap may be identified if there is a significant number of referrals that do not lead to child care placements or if there is a lack of providers available to accept these referrals. Additionally, a disparity in referrals between children with and without disabilities could indicate a gap. Collaborative Developmental Screening Activities: Data Collection: Assess the current availability and usage of developmental screening tools in child care settings and the follow-up actions taken when a screening indicates a potential disability. Gap Identification: A gap may be identified if there are insufficient screening activities, if screenings are not reaching all children (especially those in rural or underserved areas), or if there is a lack of follow-up resources or services when a developmental concern is identified. d. Children who receive care during non-traditional hours. Describe: Anecdotal information indicates that in Idaho a variety of professions such as law enforcement and the military are seeking child care solutions for care during non-traditional hours. According to a July 18, 2023 press release from Idaho Senator Mike Simpson, The National Law Enforcement Foundation is partnering to build a childcare center for law enforcement officers in the Treasure Valley to provide "safe and secure childcare and education coverage that matches the needs of law enforcement families and would meet a widely acknowledged need within Idaho law enforcement." The Idaho National Guard in Boise has also constructed a child care facility to meet the non-traditional hour child care needs of Guardsmen during their drill weekends. Additionally, the recently completed statewide needs assessment is informing future strategies for increasing access and quality of child care during non-traditional hours. In the meantime, Idaho continues to have regionally located child care consultants available to provide on-site and over-the-phone technical assistance to new and existing providers considering providing child care during non-traditional hours. Consultants have knowledge and resources available to assist providers serving children during non- traditional hours. Start up grants are available to newly enrolled child care providers. The grant is a reimbursement grant that may cover such expenses as background checks for the provider or items needed to pass their health inspection. e. Other. Specify what population is being focused on to increase supply or improve quality. Describe: IdahoSTARS is implementing internal professional development support for our coaching team to improve their ability to build responsive relationships in coaching. This activity is intended to increase the quality of coaching relationships for providers of all race/ethnicities, preferred languages, and facility types. 4.5.5 Prioritization of investments in areas of concentrated poverty and unemployment Lead Agencies must prioritize investments for increasing access to high-quality child care and development services for children of families in areas that have significant concentrations of poverty and unemployment and do not currently have sufficient numbers of such programs. Describe how the Lead Agency prioritizes increasing access to high-quality child care and development services for children of families in areas that have significant concentrations of poverty and unemployment and that do not have access to high-quality programs. An analysis was performed so that the Lead Agency could highlight the poverty information (through census data) and the child and provider level data to get an idea of where children participating in the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) were being served and what types of providers were serving the most children in correlation to which of those counties had poverty rates. Unemployment data was gathered through the Department of Labor to contribute to the analysis. Idaho plans to use this data to work with IdahoSTARS to target the areas of need and increase recruitment of providers in those high need areas. The report will also be a tool to review data during the process of conducting the market rate study. Idaho defined areas with significant concentrations of poverty and unemployment by comparing number of children in poverty by county, per number of providers available. These data were derived from the Census. Idaho does not have a waiting list for subsidized care, so all children/families in areas of significant concentrations of poverty and unemployment would have access to the Idaho Child Care Program subsidy as an option pending other eligibility criteria are met. The IdahoSTARS project, through the University of Idaho, targets child care providers who currently run businesses in identified high poverty communities to increase technical assistance and recruit current providers into enrolling in the Steps to Quality, Idaho's Quality Rating Improvement program. In efforts to recruit more providers, the CCRC staff offer start up grants to assist providers in starting their business. 5 Health and Safety of Child Care Settings Child care health and safety standards and enforcement practices are essential to protect the health and safety of children while out of their parents’ care. CCDF provides a minimum threshold for child care health and safety policies and practices but leaves authority to Lead Agencies to design standards that appropriately protect children’s safety and promote nurturing environments that support their healthy growth and development. Lead Agencies should set standards for ratios, group size limits, and provider qualifications that help ensure that the child care environment is conducive to safety and learning and enable caregivers to promote all domains of children’s development. CCDF health and safety standards help set clear expectations for CCDF providers, form the foundation for health and safety training for child care workers, and establish the baseline for monitoring to ensure compliance with health and safety requirements. These health and safety requirements apply to all providers serving children receiving CCDF services – whether the providers are licensed or license-exempt, must be appropriate to the provider setting and age of the children served, must include specific topics and training on those topics, and are subject to monitoring and enforcement procedures by the Lead Agency. CCDF-required annual monitoring and enforcement actions help ensure that CCDF providers are adopting and implementing health and safety requirements. Through child care licensing, Lead Agencies set minimum requirements, including health and safety requirements, that child care providers must meet to legally operate in that State or Territory. In some cases, CCDF health and safety requirements may be integrated within the licensing system for licensed providers and may be separate for CCDF providers who are license- exempt. This section addresses CCDF health and safety requirements, Lead Agency licensing requirements and exemptions, and comprehensive background checks. When responding to questions in this section, OCC recognizes that each Lead Agency identifies and defines its own categories of care. OCC does not expect Lead Agencies to change their definitions to fit the CCDF-defined categories of care. For these questions, provide responses that best match the CCDF categories of care.
