body: A Lead Agency must have a professional development framework for training, professional development, and post-secondary education for caregivers, teachers, and directors in child care programs that serve children of all ages. The framework must include these components: (1) professional standards and competencies, (2) career pathways, (3) advisory structures, (4) articulation, (5) workforce information, and (6) financing. CCDF provides Lead Agencies flexibility on the strategies, breadth, and depth of the framework. The professional development framework must be developed in consultation with the State Advisory Council on Early Childhood Education and Care or a similar coordinating body. 6.2.1 Updates and consultation a. Did the Lead Agency make any updates to the professional development framework since the FFY 2022-2024 CCDF Plan was submitted? [x] Yes. If yes, describe the elements of the framework that were updated and describe if and how the State Advisory Council on Early Childhood Education and Care (if applicable) or similar coordinating body was consulted: IdahoSTARS partners and collaborates with high school Career and Technical Education (CTE) programs to expose students to early childhood education, fostering student interest in pursuing careers working with young children and broadening recruitment efforts to attract a diverse pool of aspiring educators. Additionally, IdahoSTARS provides professional development opportunities for FCS (Family and Consumer Sciences) CTE teachers to effectively prepare students for careers in Early Childhood Education (ECE). Program supports including technical assistance and resources for curriculum articulation to the CDA (Child Development Associate credential) facilitate students' credentialing pathways and establish clear career trajectories in the field after graduation. Engagement with Family, Career and Community Leaders of America (FCCLA) student organization allows IdahoSTARS to introduce high school students to early childhood education careers, offering educational resources and opportunities to cultivate their interest and encourage recruitment into the industry. College scholarships available from IdahoSTARS to graduating high school seniors who are pursuing a degree or certificate at the post-secondary level lead to retention in the field. The ICCP Panel, serving as the advisory committee for IdahoSTARS, was involved in the decision making process to add the ￿Future Educator’s Scholarship’ targeted to graduating Idaho High School Seniors who have committed to pursuing a degree or certificate in Early Childhood Education, Child Development, Family and Consumer Sciences or a closely related field at an accredited Idaho institution of higher education. The advisory committee was consulted in the decision making process to add this new scholarship as this in only one of two scholarships which does not require current employment in child care for the duration of the 1-year freshman scholarship. They were crucial in the conversation to allow this employment exemption, which is a deviation to IdahoSTARS typical incentive distribution requirements in order to address workforce recruitment and retention issues. Those Future Educator Scholarship recipients who become employed in child care after their freshman year have the ability to transition to a renewable scholarship which does require continued employment in child care to maintain scholarship eligibility. [ ]No. b. Did the Lead Agency consult with other key groups in the development of their professional development framework? [x] Yes. If yes, identify the other key groups: Child care providers were the primary driver of revising the pathway as providers expressed frustration with stagnation on the pathway especially due to the pause at Level 4 due to the associate degree requirement. Idaho’s Early Childhood Higher Education Consortium, which includes faculty from all Idaho institutions of higher education with early childhood coursework and the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) Advisory Panel, which serves as the state’s CCDF advisory council was consulted in the discussion and decision making process. [ ] No. 6.2.2 Description of the professional development framework a. Describe how the Lead Agency’s framework for training and professional development addresses the following required elements: i. Professional standards and competencies. For example, Lead Agencies can include information about which roles in early childhood education are included (such as teachers, directors, infant and toddler specialists, mental health consultants, coaches, licensors, QIS assessors, family service workers, home visitors). The IdahoSTARS Quality Domains and Subcategories, which align with national standards, are used to categorize all professional development opportunities, training, targeted technical assistance and coaching. The Idaho Early Learning eGuidelines are the most current, research-based standards in Idaho. The eGuidelines are utilized in all IdahoSTARS approved trainings. ii. Career pathways. For example, Lead Agencies can include information about professional development registries, career ladders, and levels. The IdahoSTARS Early Childhood Care and Education Career Pathway contains six levels beginning with Level 1 of the Professional Development System (PDS) which reflects entry and completion of a high school diploma or equivalency. Level 2 requires a CDA (Child Development Associate) credential, Montessori credential, or 12 ECE- related college credits. Level 3 requires a technical certificate in ECE. Level 4 requires an associate degree in ECE or 30 ECE- related college credits. Level 5 requires a bachelor's degree in ECE or a bachelor’s degree in any field with 36 ECE-related college credits; Level 6 requires a master's degree or higher in ECE. International transcripts and diplomas are translated and reviewed individually to determine placement on the pathway. iii. Advisory structure. For example, Lead Agencies can include information about how the professional development advisory structure interacts with the State Advisory Council on Early Childhood Education and Care. The Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) Advisory Panel provides guidance and recommendations to both ICCP and the IdahoSTARS program. IdahoSTARS leadership works with Idaho's child care administrator and team to determine agenda items and plan for the Advisory Panel meetings, scheduled quarterly and held either in person and/or via a web-based platform to allow participation by all members of the panel. The Advisory Panel provides guidance and recommendations on the annual ICCP required training, updates and revisions to Steps to Quality, the initial and ongoing development of the RISE Application (IdahoSTARS' web-based database), revisions to the career pathway, incentives and opportunities that support the professional development for child care providers, and ongoing efforts to embed equity in our processes and practices. iv. Articulation. For example, Lead Agencies can include information about articulation agreements, and collaborative agreements that support progress in degree acquisition. The partnership and collaboration between IdahoSTARS and 2 and 4-year higher education institutions are beneficial for child care providers in Idaho. IdahoSTARS participates in the Early Childhood Education Consortium, which convenes representatives from higher education institutions and state agencies annually. These meetings provide opportunities for program updates, sharing of resources, and alignment of training and educational offerings with state frameworks and priorities. Collaborations from participation in the Higher Education Consortium have resulted in new degree programs, articulation agreements between 2 and 4- year institutions, clearer degree pathways between institutions and alignment of curriculum not only to professional standards, but to the needs of the workforce. v. Workforce information. For example, Lead Agencies can include information about workforce demographics, educator well-being, retention/turnover surveys, actual wage scales, and/or access to benefits. IdahoSTARS collects information from the early care and education workforce via our RISE Application. Beyond the management of program licensing and subsidy eligibility, the RISE Application collects demographic data on Idaho's child care workforce. Data is collected on the workforce in areas of both employment and demographics. Data collected on the workforce’s employment include wage, geographic location, child care setting and ages served, position title, and dates of employment. Personal demographic data points include highest level of education, race/ethnicity, language(s) spoken, sex, and age. Data collected from the system informs the management and equity of our programs. Where appropriate, this information is aggregated, disseminated, and utilized to inform policy makers, business owners, directors, educators, parents, child care providers, service providers, partners, among others across Idaho. Data from the system informs IdahoSTARS annual ￿State of the Child Care Workforce Report’. vi. Financing. For example, Lead Agencies can include information about strategies including scholarships, apprenticeships, wage enhancements, etc. The IdahoSTARS professional development system (PDS) offers several financial supports and incentives for eligible providers. The Early Childhood Care and Education Career Pathway offers an annual financial incentive "anniversary award" for the completion of 20 or more hours of IdahoSTARS approved training or one Early Childhood Education (ECE) college credit or related credit within their anniversary cycle. The amount of the anniversary award is tied to the provider's level on the career pathway and increases as the provider moves up levels on the pathway. Financial support of $200 in the form of training scholarships is available to every provider enrolled in the PDS and who work 15 hours or more in a center or home based child care facility. Training scholarships are used for approved professional development trainings, conferences, and other educational opportunities with an associated cost. GED testing scholarships reimburse providers for costs associated with completing GED testing. Child Development Associate (CDA) Assessment and Renewal scholarships are used to pay for costs associated with obtaining or renewing the CDA credential. Academic degree scholarships are available for providers who are working toward a degree in early childhood education at an approved Idaho college or university. Single course scholarships cover the cost of one ECE or closely related course at an approved Idaho college or university. Badge incentives are a financial recognition available to providers who complete targeted, IdahoSTARS approved professional development activities to earn an IdahoSTARS Early Childhood Badge. Seven different badges are available and providers may earn up to 2 associated financial recognitions for earning badges each fiscal year. b. Does the Lead Agency use additional elements? [x] Yes. If yes, describe the element(s). Check all that apply. i. [x] Continuing education unit trainings and credit-bearing professional development. Describe: IdahoSTARS uses the International Accreditors of Continuing Education and Training (IACET) accreditor to determine training hour equivalents to continuing education units (CEU) and academic credits. IACET- approved companies equate one CEU per ten contact/training hours, academic credits equate as one credit per 15 contact/training hours. Waldorf and Montessori programs have a variable equivalent that is based on the category of class offered. ii. [x] Engagement of training and professional development providers, including higher education, in aligning training and educational opportunities with the Lead Agency's framework. Describe: The IdahoSTARS Training Office oversees the ongoing training and professional development for child care providers in Idaho. The Training Office utilizes a system to approve trainers and training in each region, conferences, and e-learning opportunities. IdahoSTARS approved trainers and trainings reflect current research, best practice, and specialized topics. Trainings are accessible throughout the state in a variety of formats that includes live in-person, live webinar, online (e-learning), and through academic based course work. Idaho strives to meet the needs of a diverse provider and child care population by offering training in a variety of formats and utilizing the data system as a means to obtain language preferences and/or adaptations needed that allow all providers to successfully complete training classes. Idaho provides a variety of training in English and Spanish and offers interpreters for languages other than English, translation of materials for IdahoSTARS developed training, and adaptations upon request. iii. [ ] Other. Describe: [ ] No. 6.2.3 Impact of the Professional Development Framework Describe how the framework improves the quality, diversity, stability, and retention of caregivers, teachers, and directors and identify what data are available to assess the impact. a. Professional standards and competencies. For example, do the professional standards and competencies reflect the diversity of providers across role, child care setting, or age of children served? Idaho’s state standards, the Idaho Early Learning eGuidelines are designed to assist in guiding children’s development and learning for a diversity of providers, across roles, different child care settings and is based on developmental ages Birth through Grade 3. The standards are a focus in all IdahoSTARS approved training. - Children are active learners who learn through play. - Each child learns in unique ways. - Children receive learning opportunities that support their unique needs in inclusive environments. - Learning is most meaningful when it is integrated across all areas of development. --Domain 1: Approaches to Learning, Executive Functioning, and Cognitive Development --Domain 2: Physical Well-Being, Health and Motor Development --Domain 3: Social and Emotional Development --Domain 4: General Knowledge --Domain 5: Communication, Language, and Literacy IdahoSTARS Quality Domains and Subcategories are used to categorize approved trainings, target technical assistant, and coaching to ensure best practices are with the professional development offerings. The seven domains provide information for all child care providers and director/owner in a variety of settings. These domains contain content for ages Birth through 12 years. -Curriculum & Instruction -Child Development -Inclusion & Diversity -Business Practices -Health, Safety & Wellness -Environments -Partnerships with Families & Communities b. Career pathways. For example, has the Lead Agency developed a wage ladder that provides progressively higher wages as early educators gain more experience and credentials? What types of child care settings and staff roles are addressed in career pathways, such as licensed centers and family child care homes? The Career Pathway outlines specific requirements for obtaining credentials such as the Child Development Associate (CDA) credential, technical certificates in Early Childhood Education (ECE), associate degrees, bachelor's degrees, and master's degrees. By facilitating access to credentialing programs and incentivizing credential attainment, IdahoSTARS promotes diversity and professionalism within the early childhood education workforce. While IdahoSTARS may not have developed a formal wage ladder, the Career Pathway's emphasis on higher education, training, and credentials indirectly supports wage progression. As early educators gain more experience and qualifications, they become eligible for higher-paying positions within the field, contributing to stability and retention by providing opportunities for career advancement. The Career Pathway encompasses various child care settings, including licensed centers and family child care homes, as well as all staff roles. This comprehensive approach ensures that career advancement opportunities are accessible across all segments of the child care workforce. Data collected through the RISE Application includes credential attainment, workforce demographics and employment information such as wage and turnover. Analysis of the data in relation to Career Pathway participation and advancement provides insights into the diversity and inclusivity of the workforce and can assist in evaluation of the effectiveness of career advancement initiatives in retaining qualified professionals within the field. c. Advisory structure. For example, has the advisory structure identified goals for child care workforce compensation, including types of staff and target compensation levels? Does the Lead Agency have a Preschool Development Birth-to-Five grant and is part of its scope of work child care compensation activities? Are they represented in the advisory structure? The Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) Advisory Panel provides guidance and recommendations to both ICCP and the IdahoSTARS program. IdahoSTARS leadership works with Idaho's child care administrator and team to determine agenda items and plan for the Advisory Panel meetings, scheduled quarterly and held either in person and/or via a web-based platform to allow participation by all members of the panel. The Advisory Panel provides guidance and recommendations on the annual ICCP required training, updates and revisions to Steps to Quality, the initial and ongoing development of the RISE Application (IdahoSTARS' web-based database), revisions to the career pathway, incentives and opportunities that support the professional development for child care providers, and ongoing efforts to embed equity in our processes and practices. The Lead Agency is not the grantee for the Preschool Development Birth-to-Five grant, however the grantee is represented on the Idaho Child Care Advisory Panel. We do not work with any advisory group, ICCP, PDG or other regarding target compensation levels. Note that PDG is not directly aligned with CCDF recognitions, but PDG partnership activities around academic and CDA supports have been provided. d. Articulation. For example, how does the advisory structure include training and professional development for providers, including higher education, to assist in aligning training and education opportunities? The Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) Advisory Panel comprises representatives from various stakeholders, including higher education institutions, training providers, child care administrators, and IdahoSTARS leadership. This diverse representation allows for collaboration and input from key entities involved in training and education. The panel provides guidance and recommendations on a range of topics related to professional development, including training content, curriculum development, and educational opportunities. Higher education representatives contribute their expertise to ensure that training and educational offerings align with academic standards and best practices. Idaho’s legislature recently (effective January 2024) passed measures allowing and encouraging Idaho institutions of higher education to award ￿Credit for Prior Learning￿ academic credits to individuals who have achieved industry credentials Individualized assessments or experiential learning, particularly portfolio based assessments whereby students demonstrate learning acquired through experiences including but not limited to: a)Work or employment b)Employer training programs c)Independent study d)Non-credit courses e)Non-college courses or seminars f)Apprenticeships These rules apply to every school in Idaho who offers an Early Childhood Education degree or certificate pathway; decisions on how each school implements this opportunity. At this time, opportunities exist for ECE prior learning credits at the College of Western Idaho (credits for CDA credential) and Lewis Clark State College (credit for prior learning awarded through a portfolio process). IdahoSTARS continues to work on articulation and credit for prior learning through collaboration with the Idaho ECE Higher Education Consortium. e. Workforce information. For example, does the Lead Agency have data on the existing wages and benefits available to the child care workforce? Do any partners such as the Quality Improvement System, child care resource and referral agencies, Bureau of Labor Statistics, and universities and research organizations collect compensation and benefits data? Does the Lead Agency monitor child care workforce wages and access to benefits through ongoing data collection and evaluation? Can the data identify any disparities in the existing compensation and benefits (by geography, role, child care setting, race, ethnicity, gender, or age of children served)? The Lead Agency, through IdahoSTARS, monitors child care workforce wages and workforce turnover through ongoing data collection and evaluation. This involves collecting data on wages and other employment- related factors through the RISE Application and through periodic surveys of the workforce. Regular evaluation of this data allows for tracking trends over time and identifying areas for improvement. The IdahoSTARS annual publication ￿State of the Child Care Workforce Report’ examines issues of wages, turnover, and other workforce-related factors. f. Financing. For example, has the Lead Agency set a minimum or living wage as a floor for all child care staff? Do Lead Agency-provider subsidy agreements contain requirements for staff compensation levels? Do Lead Agencies provide program-level compensation grants to support staff base salaries and benefits? Does the Lead Agency administer bonuses or stipends directly to workers? IdahoSTARS does not explicitly set a minimum or living wage as a floor for all child care staff, the financing supports offered do indirectly contribute to improving wages and benefits for the workforce. By offering financial supports such as training scholarships, GED testing scholarships, academic degree scholarships, and compensation grants, IdahoSTARS helps providers increase their qualifications and potentially negotiate higher wages. Direct financial payments (bonuses) to child care workers as incentives for professional development are directly tied to retention, and quality improvement efforts. For example, the anniversary award tied to completion of training hours or college credits provides direct financial incentives to providers for investing in their professional growth. Data collected in the RISE Application includes information on wages, turnover rates, and other employment- related factors. Analysis of this data allows IdahoSTARS to assess the impact of financing initiatives on workforce stability, retention, and diversity.

body: 6.3.1 Required hours of ongoing training Provide the number of hours of ongoing training required annually for CCDF-eligible providers in the following settings: a. Licensed child care centers: Twelve (12) hours annually b. License-exempt child care centers: Idaho does not have license-exempt center child care. c. Licensed family child care homes: Twelve (12) hours annually d. License-exempt family child care homes: Twelve (12) hours annually e. Regulated or registered in-home child care: Twelve (12) hours annually f. Non-regulated or registered in-home child care: Idaho does not license in-home child care. 6.3.2 Accessibility of professional development for Tribal organizations Describe how the Lead Agency’s training and professional development are accessible to providers supported through Indian tribes or Tribal organizations receiving CCDF funds (as applicable). Idaho’s training and professional development system are open to all child care professionals, which includes all providers supported through Indian tribes or tribal organizations and who are in the field of early care and education. Within the IdahoSTARS data system training offerings are posted on an electronic training calendar as well as within the training catalog for provider’s training registration and training requests. Offerings include live in-person, live webinar, online (e- learning), approved company, and targeted technical assistance/coaching for professional development hours. Individuals who are unaware of or do not utilize the data system are able to access the IdahoSTARS website where information is available on how to join the Professional Development System, how to create an account in the data system, and how to access other opportunities. 6.3.3 Professional development appropriate for the diversity of children, families, and child care providers Describe how the Lead Agency’s training and professional development requirements reflect the diversity of children, families, and child care providers participating in CCDF. To the extent practicable, how does professional development include specialized training or credentials for providers who care for infants or school-age children; individuals with limited English proficiency; children who are bilingual; children with developmental delays or disabilities; and/or Native Americans, including Indians, as the term is defined in Section 900.6 in subpart B of the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (including Alaska Natives) and Native Hawaiians? IdahoSTARS training (live, webinar, and eLearning), targeted technical assistance, and coaching are offered within the Quality Domain of Inclusion & Diversity: Access-provides a wide range of activities and environments for every child by removing physical barriers and offering multiple ways to promote learning, Participation-uses a range of instructional approaches to promote engagement in play and learning activities, and a sense of belonging for every child, Supports- refers to broader aspects of the system such as professional development, incentives for inclusion, and opportunities for communication and collaboration among families and professionals to assure high quality inclusion, and Diversity-the program support children’s social and cultural identity as it relates to race, color, religion, sex, income level, national origin, and home language. IdahoSTARS live in-person and webinars offer child care providers interpreters as needed to ensure a better learning experience. Infant and Toddler Mental Health: Recognizing the critical importance of mental health in early childhood, providers are encouraged to pursue specialized training and recognition to obtain the Infant and Family Associate (IFA) Endorsement category recognized by the Alliance. • In partnership with AIM Early Idaho, IdahoSTARS IFA endorsed team members support child care providers in reviewing their professional development record (PDR) to identify gaps and recognize strengths. These IdahoSTARS team members develop training plans and support the provider through the application process. IdahoSTARS endorsed team members also act as endorsement reviewers, reviewing and recommending applicants from other entities in Idaho for endorsement. Providers are also assisted with a Pyramid Model Crosswalk and RISE Application crosswalk of approved trainings that meet the required competencies required to earn endorsement. •Through intentional training opportunities IdahoSTARS highly trained team members offer training, coaching, and Targeted Technical Assistance (TTA) on infant and toddler mental health through the Pyramid Model, Zero to Three Critical Competency training, and other identified training in our RISE Application. IdahoSTARS equips providers with the knowledge and skills to promote healthy social-emotional development in infants, identify early signs of mental health concerns, and support families in nurturing their child’s emotional wellbeing. IdahoSTARS live in-person and webinars offer child care providers interpreters as needed as well as any accommodation (Visual, Hearing, or Mobility) to ensure the best learning experience. All IdahoSTARS developed training, eLearning or PowerPoint, are developed using accessibility best practice for all learners. Every training developer must create their training with the lens of adaptations for the content to support all children and deliver these supports during the training. IdahoSTARS also offers many eLearning opportunities in Spanish with more being translated each year. To better address the needs of specific populations, IdahoSTARS offers a comprehensive array of professional development opportunities that include specialized training and credentials tailored to providers who care for infants, school-age children, individuals with limited English proficiency, children who are bilingual, children with developmental disabilities or delays, and Native American children, including Indians, as the term is defined in Section 900.6 in subpart B of the Indian Self- Determination and Education Assistance Act (including Alaska Natives) and Native Hawaiians. Here's a more detailed and specific description of how IdahoSTARS incorporates these elements into its training and support services: IdahoSTARS Training and Support for Diverse Populations General Overview: IdahoSTARS provides a robust professional development framework within the Quality Domain of Inclusion & Diversity, encompassing Access, Participation, Supports, and Diversity. These initiatives are designed to ensure that every child has access to high-quality early childhood education, irrespective of their background or developmental needs. The training is delivered through live sessions, webinars, and eLearning, with additional targeted technical assistance and coaching. Specialized Training and Credentials: 1. Infants and Toddlers: Infant and Family Associate (IFA) Endorsement: IdahoSTARS encourages providers who work with infants to pursue specialized training in infant mental health, including the IFA Endorsement recognized by the Alliance. This endorsement emphasizes the importance of early childhood mental health and equips providers with the skills to support infants' social-emotional development. Partnership with Aim Early Idaho: IFA-endorsed team members assist providers in reviewing their Professional Development Record (PDR) to identify gaps, develop training plans, and support the application process for endorsement. These team members also serve as endorsement reviewers, ensuring that applicants from across Idaho meet the required competencies. Pyramid Model and Zero to Three Training: IdahoSTARS provides training on the Pyramid Model and Zero to Three Critical Competencies, focusing on promoting healthy social-emotional development, identifying early signs of mental health concerns, and supporting families in nurturing their infants' emotional well-being. 2. School-Age Children: Developmentally Appropriate Practices: IdahoSTARS offers training on developmentally appropriate practices for school-age children, emphasizing engagement in learning activities that foster a sense of belonging. Providers learn to create inclusive environments that accommodate the varied needs of school-age children, ensuring their participation and success in child care settings. 3. Individuals with Limited English Proficiency and Bilingual Children: Culturally Responsive Training: IdahoSTARS provides specialized training to equip providers with strategies for supporting children who have limited English proficiency or are bilingual. This includes offering interpreters during live and webinar training sessions to enhance learning experiences for providers. Training emphasizes creating inclusive environments that honor and support the linguistic and cultural identities of these children. Language Support: The training and technical assistance offered by IdahoSTARS focus on developing instructional approaches that facilitate language acquisition and support bilingualism, promoting participation and engagement in the learning process. Diverse Classroom Materials: Providers are trained on selecting culturally diverse books and materials that reflect the backgrounds of the children they serve, promoting a sense of belonging and cultural identity. 4. Children with Developmental Disabilities or Delays: Inclusion and Accessibility Training: IdahoSTARS offers professional development on inclusive practices that address the needs of children with developmental disabilities or delays. This includes training on modifying environments, adapting instructional methods, and utilizing assistive technologies to remove barriers to participation and learning. Collaboration with Families: Providers are trained to collaborate closely with families and other professionals to develop individualized support plans that promote the full inclusion of children with disabilities in all aspects of the child care environment. EC Series by SESTA: This series includes Early Care and Education Environment Indicators for Inclusion, which guide providers in adapting their environments to meet the needs of all children. 5. Native American Children, Including Indigenous Populations: IdahoSTARS offers training that emphasizes the importance of understanding and respecting the cultural identities. This includes fostering an environment that supports these children’s social and cultural identity, including their language, traditions, and values. Continuous Support and Professional Development Technical Assistance and Coaching: IdahoSTARS offers ongoing support through targeted technical assistance (TTA) and coaching to help providers apply what they have learned in their professional development. This ensures that training is not just theoretical but also practical and impactful in everyday childcare settings. Collaborative Opportunities: Providers are encouraged to engage in communication and collaboration with families and other professionals to ensure the highest quality of inclusive care, reflecting the diverse backgrounds and needs of the children in their care. 6.3.4 Child developmental screening Describe how all providers receive, through training and professional development, information about: (1) existing resources and services the State/Territory can make available in conducting developmental screenings and providing referrals to services when appropriate for children who receive assistance under this part, including the coordinated use of the Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnosis, and Treatment program (42 U.S.C. 1396 et seq.) and developmental screening services available under section 619 and part C of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (20 U.S.C. 1419, 1431 et seq.); and (2) how child care providers may utilize these resources and services to obtain developmental screenings for children who receive assistance and who may be at risk for cognitive or other developmental delays, which may include social, emotional, physical, or linguistic delays: Child Care Providers are introduced to developmental screenings through the Idaho Child Care Program In-office Orientation (IIO) as they decide to become an ICCP provider. IdahoSTARS has embedded an emerging indicator in our state quality and rating improvement system inclusive of the use of developmental monitoring and screening. Child care providers engaged with the Idaho Pyramid Model Collaborative begin using developmental screeners as a component of their roadmap in Year 2 or Year 3 of our three year roadmap. Providers additional have access to training and Targeted Technical Assistance (TTA) associated with developmental screeners specifically the ASQ 3 and ASQ SE 2. General information on developmental screening is located on the IdahoSTARS website in the Basics of Child Development tab.

body: Lead Agencies must develop, maintain, or implement early learning and developmental guidelines appropriate for children from birth to kindergarten entry. Early learning and developmental guidelines should describe what children should know and be able to do at different ages and cover the essential domains of early childhood development, which at a minimum includes cognition, including language arts and mathematics; social, emotional, and physical development; and approaches toward learning. 6.4.1 Early learning and developmental guidelines a. Check the boxes below to certify the Lead Agency’s early learning and developmental guidelines are: i. [x] Research-based. ii. [x] Developmentally appropriate. iii. [x] Culturally and linguistically appropriate. iv. [x] Aligned with kindergarten entry. v. [x] Appropriate for all children from birth to kindergarten entry. vi. [x] Implemented in consultation with the educational agency and the State Advisory Council on Early Childhood Education and Care or similar coordinating body. vii. If any components above are not checked, describe: NA b. Check the boxes below to certify that the required domains are included in the Lead Agency’s early learning and developmental guidelines. i. [x] Cognition, including language arts and mathematics. ii. [x] Social development. iii. [x] Emotional development. iv. [x] Physical development. v. [x] Approaches toward learning. vi. [ ] Other optional domains. Describe any optional domains: vii. If any components above are not checked, describe: NA c. When were the Lead Agency’s early learning and developmental guidelines most recently updated and for what reason? The Office of Head Start is currently the lead on development and updates for the Early Learning and Development Guidelines. The Idaho Early Learning Guidelines were revised in 2020-2021 and are reviewed every 5 years. d. Provide the Web link to the Lead Agency's early learning and developmental guidelines. https://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/services-programs/about-idaho-early-learning- eguidelines 6.4.2 Use of early learning and developmental guidelines a. Describe how the Lead Agency uses its early learning and developmental guidelines. The state of Idaho created the Idaho Early Learning eGuidelines, the latest set of high quality, research-based Idaho early learning standards for children from birth through kindergarten. The latest revision of the eGuidelines (2019-2020) are a culmination of a two-year study and revision process by a statewide team of early childhood experts, professionals, and higher education faculty. The eGuidelines provides a common language and framework for discussing and describing young children's typical growth. The eGuidelines are used to guide policy, pre-service and in-service development, and best practice at all levels of early childhood. These eGuidelines have been adopted as Idaho's Early Learning Standards for Idaho's Special Education Preschool programs. In addition, they are carefully aligned with Head Start/Early Head Start School Readiness goals, and the Head Start Early Learning Framework. The eGuidelines offer guidance on child development from birth to kindergarten for schools, Head Start programs, parents, child care providers, and professional development organizations. In addition, the eGuidelines expand and support the K-12 Common Core Standards by addressing early social and emotional development and approaches to learning and cognitive development through the primary grades. These address key developmental issues that are necessary for successful learning and are used extensively by our early special educators in the development of individual education plans. Each domain addressed in the eGuidelines specifically highlight "Supporting Individual Differences, Languages, and Diversity" noting that cultural and linguistic experiences shape development, Caregiver Strategies offer guidance on cultural variations in behavior and language. These guidelines were vetted through the Idaho Child Care Program Advisory Panel. Through the support of the Early Childhood Coordinating Council (EC3) and the Head Start Collaboration office, collateral products were developed for infants and toddlers and for preschool aged children. These materials were disseminated to child care providers across the state by IdahoAEYC and Child Care Resource and Referral staff. IdahoSTARS approved training are required to reference the Early Learning eGuidelines and trainers include the connection of their training to the eGuidelines during their presentations. The intention is to help build capacity of child care providers to access the online tool when planning their classroom activities. b. Check the boxes below to certify that CCDF funds are not used to develop or implement an assessment for children that: i. [x] Will be the primary or sole basis to determine a child care provider ineligible to participate in the CCDF. ii. [x] Will be used as the primary or sole basis to provide a reward or sanction for an individual provider. iii. [x] Will be used as the primary or sole method for assessing program effectiveness. iv. [x] Will be used to deny children eligibility to participate in CCDF. v. If any components above are not checked, describe: NA 7 Quality Improvement Activities The quality of child care directly affects children’s safety and healthy development while in care settings, and high-quality child care can be foundational across the lifespan. Lead Agencies may use CCDF for quality improvement activities for all children in care, not just those receiving child care subsidies. OCC will collect the most detailed Lead Agency information about quality improvement activities in annual reports instead of this Plan. Lead Agencies must report on CCDF child care quality improvement investments in three ways: 1. In this Plan, Lead Agencies will describe the types of activities supported by quality investments over the 3-year period. 2. An annual expenditure report (the ACF-696). Lead Agencies will provide data on how much CCDF funding is spent on quality activities. This report will be used to determine compliance with the required quality and infant and toddler spending requirements. 3. An annual Quality Progress Report (the ACF-218). Lead Agencies will provide a description of activities funded by quality expenditures, the measures used to evaluate its progress in improving the quality of child care programs and services within the State/Territory, and progress or barriers encountered on those measures. In this section of the Plan, Lead Agencies will describe their quality activities needs assessment and identify the types of quality improvement activities where CCDF investments are being made using quality set-aside funds.

body: 7.1.1 Needs assessment process and findings a. Describe the Lead Agency needs assessment process for expending CCDF funds on activities to improve the quality of child care, including the frequency of assessment, how a diverse range of parents and providers were consulted, and how their views are incorporated: IdahoSTARS engages child care providers through a variety of beneficiary voice activities to support the project’s program development, guide our implementation, and gauge our impact. It is through beneficiary voice activities that we understand the needs of child care providers in our state. Beneficiary voice activities can involve general or targeted groups of child care providers participating in listening sessions, interviews, surveys, and the completion of feedback loops. Steps to Quality, the state’s Quality Rating and Improvement System (QRIS), has utilized all forms of beneficiary voice activities to inform a QRIS restructure. Utilizing beneficiary voice activities with child care providers has contributed to our understanding of how our QRIS can better meet the needs of child care programs. IdahoSTARS is committed to utilizing beneficiary voice in our process to identify the needs of child care providers. We regularly hold listening session wherein we engage child care providers with broad, open-ended questions about our supports and services. We respect their expertise as users of our systems and use their feedback to inform our decision making. Providers are invited to listening session via email and phone call. The transcripts of the listening sessions are reviewed by teams of staff members to identify common themes, the themes are then sent out to the listening session participants to confirm that we are correctly interpreting their feedback. Then we use those themes to inform our decision making. b. Describe the findings of the assessment, including any findings related to needs of different populations and types of providers, and if any overarching goals for quality improvement were identified: Through our Beneficiary Voice Activities, we have identified the following overarching needs from providers: 1. Child care providers want their work to be valued and supported by their peers, directors, families and IdahoSTARS. 2. Child care providers value professional development as a Providers have distinct communication preferences and when IdahoSTARS is unaware of those preferences, users do not ￿receive’ information that is important to them. 3. Child care providers value the RISE Application as a tool. They have concerns about the ease of navigation based on language preference, access to technology & technological fluency. 4. Providers also have recommendations for improvement ways to learn new information, refresh knowledge and improve their skills/practice in order to better serve their families. 5. Financial incentives are helpful and motivating. Incentives make providers feel recognized and appreciated. 6. Providers find value in relationship based supports like coaching and TTA. These supports are valuable when they are consistent, responsive, reliable, well-informed and able to provide personalized support. 7. Providers struggle to navigate IdahoSTARS systems without individualized support from an IdahoSTARS staff member. During our listening sessions we have identified the following needs: 1. Child care providers want their work to be valued and supported by their peers, directors, families and IdahoSTARS. 2. Child care providers value professional development as a way to learn new information, refresh knowledge and improve their skills/practice in order to better serve their families. 3. Financial incentives are helpful and motivating. Incentives make providers feel recognized and appreciated. 4. Providers find value in relationship based supports like coaching and TTA. These supports are valuable when they are consistent, responsive, reliable, well-informed and able to provide personalized support. 5. Providers struggle to navigate IdahoSTARS systems without individualized support from an IdahoSTARS staff member. 6. Providers have distinct communication preferences and when IdahoSTARS is unaware of those preferences, users do not ￿receive’ information that is important to them. 7. Child care providers value the RISE Application as a tool. They have concerns about the ease of navigation based on language preference, access to technology & technological fluency. Providers also have recommendations for improvement.

body: Lead Agencies must use a portion of their CCDF expenditures for activities designed to improve the quality of child care services and to increase parental options for and access to high-quality child care. They must use the quality set-aside funds on at least one of 10 activities described in CCDF and the quality activities must be aligned with a Statewide or Territory-wide assessment of the State's or Territory’s need to carry out such services and care. 7.2.1 Quality improvement activities a. Describe how the Lead Agency will make its Quality Progress Report (ACF – 218) and expenditure reports, available to the public. Provide a link if available. Idaho’s annual Quality Progress Report is published annually at this website: https://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/providers/child-care-providers/child-care-resources Annual program expenditures are reported in Idaho’s Fact, Figures, and Trends reports published here: https://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/about-dhw/facts-figures-and-trends b. Identify Lead Agency plans, if any, to spend CCDF funds for each of the following quality improvement activities. If an activity is checked “yes”, describe the Lead Agency’s current and/or future plans for this activity. i. Supporting the training and professional development of the child care workforce, including birth to five and school-age providers. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. Professional Development Specialist staff positions for development and delivery of training and targeted technical assistance across the state. Professional Development System Annual incentives for recognition of child care providers achievements. Training Scholarships to assist child care providers access of training opportunities. Badge Recognitions to acknowledge child care providers professional development attainment. Cohorts Recognitions to enhance the knowledge and skills obtained. Regional office Quality Consultant staff coach providers in early childhood best practices. New targeted technical assistance modules are developed and delivered each year. ii. Developing, maintaining, or implementing early learning and developmental guidelines. [x] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [ ] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. iii. Developing, implementing, or enhancing a quality improvement system. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. IdahoSTARS will continue to utilize the state’s current Quality Rating and Improvement System (QRIS), Steps to Quality. Steps to Quality is a six-step block system available to licensed and subsidy-certified child care facilities and Head Starts. IdahoSTARS has been engaging in internal and external listening sessions and workgroups for several years with the eventual goal of a launching a restructured QRIS system. iv. Improving the supply and quality of child care services for infants and toddlers. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. Our current and future investments in activities such as Infant and Toddler Mental Health endorsement, Reflective Consultation, and Critical Competency training are crucial steps towards enhancing the quality of child care for our youngest learners. By allocating resources to support our staff in these specialized areas, we are not only investing in their professional development but also ensuring that they are equipped with the latest knowledge and skills. Collaborating with national partners further amplifies these efforts, allowing us to provide cutting-edge training and resources that ultimately benefit the well-being and development of infants and toddlers in Idaho. v. Establishing or expanding a statewide system of CCR&R services. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. Idaho maintains a robust statewide system of CCR&R services. We would like to expand our Professional Development Specialists Position to include 1 to 2 more positions. This will support the delivery of targeted technical assistance and training. vi. Facilitating compliance with Lead Agency child care licensing, monitoring, inspection and health and safety standards. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x]Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. Regional offices deliver Initial Idaho Child Care Program Orientations (IIO) that focus on compliance with licensing, monitoring, inspection, and health and safety standards. Child care Health Consultants respond to referrals for follow up on coaching from Health Inspectors and work with Providers to come into compliance. Idaho Child Care Program providers are required to take initial trainings focusing on Health and Safety Standards. These trainings are updated every three years. Providers are also required to take the annual training which IdahoSTARS develops each year and typically focuses on Health and Safety. General coaching from child care Health Consultants is often related to best practice in health and safety including compliance standards. vii. Evaluating and assessing the quality and effectiveness of child care services within the State/Territory. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. IdahoSTARS uses a six-step Quality Rating and Improvement System (QRIS) to evaluate and assess the quality of participating child care facilities. Participation is voluntary and requires the facility is licensed and subsidy certified. The QRIS, Steps to Quality, utilizes a suite of Environment Rating Scales (ERS) to assess the participating programs, plus an annual verification of the programs quality practices that results in a quality rating. All programs at Steps 2-5 receive an annual ERS assessment. Minimum scores are required for rating at Steps 3-5. The block verification for a step rating consists of 79 quality indicators that result in a rating of Steps 1-5. Step 6 is a fast- track rating for programs with a current accreditation or Head Start grant. viii. Accreditation support. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. IdahoSTARS supports programs on the way to and in maintaining national accreditation in a couple of ways. IdahoSTARS offers Quality Improvement grants for programs rated at Steps 2-6 requiring materials or training to meet their quality improvement goals, including but not limited to creating an environment that meets accreditation standards. IdahoSTARS also offers an accreditation grant for programs at Steps 3- 6 that covers the cost of fees associated with national accreditation including self- study, application for accreditation or renewal. ix. Supporting State/Territory or local efforts to develop high-quality program standards relating to health, mental health, nutrition, physical activity, and physical development. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. The IdahoSTARS QRIS system, Steps to Quality, currently uses 79 quality indicators to verify a program’s quality step. The quality indicators span all seven of IdahoSTARS quality domains: Business Practices, Health, Safety and Wellness, Environments, Child Development, Curriculum and Instruction, Inclusion and Diversity, and Partnerships with Families and Communities. x. Other activities determined by the Lead Agency to improve the quality of child care services and the measurement of outcomes related to improved provider preparedness, child safety, child well-being, or kindergarten entry. [ ] No plans to spend in this category of activities at this time. [x] Yes. If yes, describe current and future investments. Child Care Health Consultants coach providers in filling out emergency plans. IdahoSTARS coaches work individually with providers in emergency planning, safety, and well-being. These coaching sessions are logged into RISE Application. IdahoSTARS also has an emergency planning targeted technical assistance module that providers can request. 8 Lead Agency Coordination and Partnerships to Support Service Delivery Coordination and partnerships help ensure that the Lead Agency’s efforts accomplish CCDF goals effectively, leverage other resources, and avoid duplication of effort. Such coordination and partnerships can help families better access child care, can assist in providing consumer education to parents, and can be used to improve child care quality and the stability of child care providers. Such coordination can also be particularly helpful in the aftermath of disasters when the provision of emergency child care services and the rebuilding and restoring of child care infrastructure are an essential part of ensuring the well-being of children and families in recovering communities. This section identifies who the Lead Agency collaborates with to implement services, how match and maintenance-of-effort (MOE) funds are used, coordination with child care resource and referral (CCR&R) systems, and efforts for disaster preparedness and response plans to support continuity of operations in response to emergencies.
heading: 7.2 Use of Quality Set-Aside Funds

body: Lead Agencies must coordinate child care services supported by CCDF with other federal, State/Territory, and local level programs. This includes programs for the benefit of Indian children, infants and toddlers, children with disabilities, children experiencing homelessness, and children in foster care. 8.1.1 Coordination with required and optional partners Describe how the Lead Agency coordinates and the results of this coordination of the provision of child care services with the organizations and agencies to expand accessibility and continuity of care and to assist children enrolled in early childhood programs in receiving full-day services that meet the needs of working families. The Lead Agency must coordinate with the following agencies: a. State Advisory Council on Early Childhood Education and Care or similar coordinating body (pursuant to 642B(b)(I)(A)(i) of the Head Start Act). Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: The Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) Advisory Panel serves as the state council for both CCDF and Head Start to improve the quality of child care by linking services for children when possible and aligning systems to enhance services. The results of aligning systems is a more efficient and accessible program for Idaho families and providers, who access ICCP subsidy and IdahoSTARS services. b. Indian Tribe(s) and/or Tribal organization(s), at the option of the Tribe or Tribal organization. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination, including which Tribe(s) was (were) involved: The State will continue to partner with all Tribes that share borders with Idaho. The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (IDHW) meets quarterly with all Tribes to ensure communication is happening both ways around programmatic information and policy changes. We use both the IDHW-wide meetings as well as the Idaho Child Care Program Advisory Panel meeting as avenues for sharing information, gathering feedback and providing opportunities for alignment where necessary. These actions results in stronger relationships with Tribal Nations which in turn allow us both to serve children and families to the best of our collective services. [ ] Not applicable. Check here if there are no Indian Tribes and/or Tribal organizations in the State/Territory. c. State/Territory agency(ies) responsible for programs for children with disabilities, including early intervention programs authorized under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: The Lead Agency sits on the Infant Toddler Advisory Council with both Part C and 619 state leads. The CCDF administrator sits on the Infant Toddler Sub Committee for transitioning of children and coordinates inter-program efforts to share information and develop plans for linking comprehensive services between infant toddler, child care and school transitions. This results in a shared language across programs and clear expectations of programs for parents who participate in the programs identified. d. State/Territory office/director for Head Start State collaboration. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: The Head Start collaboration director sits on the ICCP Advisory Panel. The CCDF administrator and Head Start collaboration director meet regularly to discuss information between both programs, problem solve and develop long range plans for partnership. The CCDF administrator worked in partnership with the Head Start collaboration director to develop both the CCDF and Head Start grant applications with the focus on collaboration and alignment of activities to strengthen knowledge and understanding around CCDF and Head Start systems. Long term goals include: (1) Increasing enrollment of Head Start programs within Idaho's Steps to Quality program; and (2) aligning Head Start and Subsidy as an expanded effort to improve the standards around health and safety and staff qualifications of child care staff to better align with Head Start. e. State/Territory agency responsible for public health, including the agency responsible for immunizations. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: Quarterly meetings are held with the Health District state lead, the CCDF program, Licensing, and 2- 1-1 Careline to share information on changes, problem solving situations, and coordination of efforts for a more streamlined process for providers and families. IdahoSTARS child care health consultants (CCHC) work closely with each regional public health office to coordinate efforts in training, outreach and Idaho technical assistance regarding public health issues including immunizations, health and safety inspections, etc. f. State/Territory agency responsible for employment services/workforce development. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: Both Employment Services and Child Care share the goal of ensuring that employment opportunities taking place within Idaho are being developed in tandem with the child care infrastructure to support families seeking care for their children as they relocate for these jobs. Reviewing workforce data and poverty levels as a component to community assessments will be critical in placement of jobs and recruitment of businesses. These efforts results in more families having access to child care programming as well as workforce and child care working together to recruit new child care businesses in areas of need, as identified through shared data evaluation. g. State/Territory agency responsible for public education, including pre-Kindergarten. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: The Lead Agency is part of efforts to align and coordinate services where possible with both McKinney-Vento and 619, both programs within the State Department of Education (SDE). State funded prekindergarten is not available in Idaho, so the partnership with the SDE pertains only to McKinney-Vento and 619. The goal is to improve access to and alignment with McKinney- Vento services between the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare and the SDE. The process will be accomplished via cross training staff and teams throughout the state and providing professional development opportunities for teachers on how best to serve families experiencing homelessness. These efforts result in more unhoused children having access to child care and school districts knowing what resources are available for serving families. h. State/Territory agency responsible for child care licensing. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: Idaho state licensing is housed under the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP). Alignment of programming and services is a comprehensive aspect of the daily work of ICCP and all aspects of provider management. IdahoSTARS assists providers in starting and renewing child care licenses and Health Districts monitor to the health and safety requirements. Together in coordination, all three entities (DHW, IdahoSTARS, Health Districts) contribute to the execution of a license. Idaho's data system is coordinated, so providers upload all content in one location, even though various entities contribute to the components of compliance. This results in streamlined efforts for the provider, through simplified review and processing of all required documents, clear communication and availability of information at any point for a provider. i. State/Territory agency responsible for the Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) and other relevant nutrition programs. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: CACFP sponsoring organizations such as St. Vincent de Paul administer the CACFP for child care homes, affiliated and unaffiliated child care centers, after school programs, and youth emergency shelters. For independent center sponsors, the responsibility for the CACFP lies with the State Department of Education, Child Nutrition Programs. The Lead Agency works with CACFP sponsoring organizations to promote and articulate CACFP education for providers. The goal of this coordination is to ensure all providers have nutritional information and/or subsidies in order to ensure children are provided nutritious snacks and meals and that parents are educated and have access to adequate nutrition. The Lead Agency ensures that all subsidized providers receive information about voluntary CACFP participation. j. McKinney-Vento State coordinators for homeless education and other agencies providing services for children experiencing homelessness and, to the extent practicable, local McKinney-Vento liaisons. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: The CCDF administrator and McKinney-Vento coordinator sit on various state councils together, and they strive to coordinate meetings when mutually beneficial to share information and develop resources and tools that can assist both statewide coordinators in the schools and community partners serving families in local communities \who are experiencing homelessness. k. State/Territory agency responsible for the TANF program. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: The Lead Agency is a part of the same state Department and Division responsible for TANF administration. In Idaho, the CCDF Administrator also serves as the TANF Administrator. Our goal is to coordinate meetings when necessary to improve access and continuity of care for children served by our two programs. Child care assistance is currently provided to families participating in the work services program mandatory for cash assistance families. l. State/Territory agency responsible for Medicaid and the State Children’s Health Insurance Program. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: The Lead Agency is a part of the same state Department and Division responsible for the state Children’s Health Insurance Program and Medicaid eligibility determination. Our goal is to coordinate meetings when necessary to share information and develop plans on a per-topic basis. m. State/Territory agency responsible for mental health services. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: The Lead Agency is a part of the same state Department responsible for Mental Health. Our goal is to coordinate meetings when necessary to improve access and continuity of care for children, served by our two programs. n. Child care resource and referral agencies, child care consumer education organizations, and providers of early childhood education training and professional development. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: Child care resource centers (CCRC) are present in all seven regions of Idaho targeted at providing resources and education to both families and child care providers. CCRC staff provides technical assistance and coaching to child care providers enrolled in the state’s Quality Ratings and Improvement System (QRIS) to improve the quality of care, expand accessibility and continuity of care, and assist children enrolled in early childhood programs to receive full- day services. The Lead Agency partners with the CCRCs through the implementation of activities as defined within the statewide contract with the University of Idaho. CCRCs are a part of IdahoSTARS, the state project working to improve the quality of child care, as defined by the Department. o. Statewide afterschool network or other coordinating entity for out-of-school time care (if applicable). Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: The Director of the Idaho Out-of-School Network sits on the ICCP Advisory Panel. The coordination goals for Idaho’s Out-of-School Network are the following: Increase awareness about and access for out-of-school programs Organize policy and partnerships for out-of-school programs Nurture quality and professional development for out-of-school programs This is completed through partnership between a statewide coalition, made up of leaders in Idaho, for which the Child Care Administrator is one participant. The process of aligning professional development for out-of-school programs with child care’s Step to Quality (STQ) Program ensures consistency and a clear pathway for all programs serving children birth to age 13. STQ is a voluntary system for child care centers and home-based programs. Programs participating in STQ work with regional quality consultants to assess, improve, and communicate quality practices p. Agency responsible for emergency management and response. Describe the coordination and results of the coordination: The Lead Agency is a part of the state's emergency management and response team. Our goal is to coordinate meetings with our Lead Agency coordinator when necessary to share information and develop plans on a per- topic basis. q. The following are examples of optional partners a Lead Agency might coordinate with to provide services. Check which optional partners the Lead Agency coordinates with and describe the coordination and results of the coordination. i. [x] State/Territory/local agencies with Early Head Start – Child Care Partnership grants. Describe: The Lead Agency works alongside the Head Start office to continue education and knowledge building around the benefits of the Early Head Start - Child Care partnership. The long range goal is to increase the number of partnerships if given the opportunity to expand in future years. ii. [x] State/Territory institutions for higher education, including community colleges. Describe: IdahoSTARS is a joint project between the University of Idaho's (UIdaho) Center on Disabilities and Human Development (CDHD) and the Idaho Association for the Education of Young Children (Idaho AEYC). The project is funded by the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (IDHW) through the Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG). A function of the responsibilities of IdahoSTARS is to advance scholarships and incentives for students in early childhood education across Idaho's two- and four-year higher education institutions, headed by the director of academics and certifications on the IdahoSTARS project. iii. [ ] Other federal, State, local, and/or private agencies providing early childhood and school-age/youth-serving developmental services. Describe: iv. [x] State/Territory agency responsible for implementing the Maternal, Infant, and Early Childhood Home Visiting (MIECHV) programs grant. Describe: The CCDF administrator sits on the statewide advisory panel for the Maternal, Infant, and Early Childhood Home Visiting (MICHV) Program. The goal is to increase the number of children receiving early intervention programming and continuity of care as families make progress through the years with their children. We are striving to increase collaboration and coordination of shared resources to professionals in the field of early care and education. v. [ ] Agency responsible for Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment Program. Describe: vi. [x] State/Territory agency responsible for child welfare. Describe: The Lead Agency is a part of the same state Department responsible for Child Welfare. Our goal is to coordinate meetings when necessary to improve access and continuity of care for children served by our two programs. Child Care partners with Child Welfare in determining eligibility for foster children in need of child care services. Specifically, children in state licensed foster homes have a streamlined eligibility process with a simplified application that does not count the foster parents' income when determining co-pays or eligibility for the foster child. This partnership is defined in an agreement, and when processes or procedures change, both divisions coordinate communication and training strategies. vii. [ ] Child care provider groups or associations. Describe: viii. [ ] Parent groups or organizations. Describe: ix. [ ] Title IV B 21st Century Community Learning Center Coordinators. Describe: x. [ ] Other. Describe:
heading: 8.1 Coordination with Partners to Expand Accessibility and Continuity of Care

body: Lead Agencies may combine CCDF funds with other Federal, State, and local child care and early childhood development programs, including those in 8.1.1. These programs include preschool programs, Tribal child care programs, and other early childhood programs, including those serving infants and toddlers with disabilities, children experiencing homelessness, and children in foster care. Combining funds may include blending multiple funding streams, pooling funds, or layering funds from multiple funding streams to expand and/or enhance services for infants, toddlers, preschoolers, and school-age children and families to allow for the delivery of comprehensive quality care that meets the needs of children and families. For example, Lead Agencies may use multiple funding sources to offer grants or contracts to programs to deliver services; a Lead Agency may allow a county/local government to use coordinated funding streams; or policies may be in place that allow local programs to layer CCDF funds with additional funding sources to pay for full-day, full-year child care that meets Early Head Start/Head Start Program Performance Standards or State/Territory pre-Kindergarten requirements in addition to State/Territory child care licensing requirements. As a reminder, CCDF funds may be used in collaborative efforts with Head Start and Early Head Start programs to provide comprehensive child care and development services for children who are eligible for both programs. 8.2.1 Combining funding for CCDF services Does the Lead Agency combine funding for CCDF services with Title XX of the Social Services Block Grant (SSBG), Title IV B 21st Century Community Learning Center Funds, State-only child care funds, TANF direct funds for child care not transferred into CCDF, Title IV-B, IV-E funds, or other federal or State programs? [ ] No. (If no, skip to question 8.2.2) [x] Yes. i. If yes, describe which funds you will combine. Combined funds may include, but are not limited to: [x] Title XX (Social Services Block Grant, SSBG) [ ] Title IV B 21st Century Community Learning Center Funds (Every Student Succeeds Act) [ ] State- or Territory-only child care funds [x] TANF direct funds for child care not transferred into CCDF [ ] Title IV-B funds (Social Security Act) [ ] Title IV-E funds (Social Security Act) [ ] Other. Describe: ii. If yes, what does the Lead Agency use combined funds to support, such as extending the day or year of services available (i.e., full-day, full-year programming for working families), smoothing transitions for children, enhancing and aligning quality of services, linking comprehensive services to children in child care, or developing the supply of child care for vulnerable populations? Idaho defines "combine" as using CCDF in combination with other allocated funding sources to serve eligible children. Idaho combines the Social Services Block Grant (SSBG), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program, and State General Funds. 8.2.2 Funds used to meet CCDF matching and MOE requirements Lead Agencies may use public funds and donated funds to meet CCDF match and maintenance of effort (matching MOE) requirements. Note: Lead Agencies that use State pre-Kindergarten funds to meet matching requirements must check State pre-Kindergarten funds and public and/or private funds. Use of private funds for match or maintenance-of-effort: Donated funds do not need to be under the administrative control of the Lead Agency to qualify as an expenditure for federal match. However, Lead Agencies must identify and designate in the State/Territory CCDF Plan the donated funds given to public or private entities to implement the CCDF child care program. [ ] Not applicable. The Lead Agency is a Territory (skip to 8.3.1). a. Does the Lead Agency use public funds to meet match requirements? [x] Yes. If yes, describe which funds are used: To meet the CCDF MOE and match requirements, the Lead Agency will use state general funds spent on child care expenses beyond those covered by the Idaho Child Care Program for children in foster care. Additionally, state general funds spent by local school districts on the administration of non-compulsory kindergarten and early literacy initiatives will be used for match in accordance with the federal limitations on public pre-kindergarten funds. [ ] No. b. Does the Lead Agency use donated funds to meet match requirements? [x] Yes. If yes, identify the entity(ies) designated to receive donated funds: i. [ ] Donated directly to the state. ii. [x] Donated to a separate entity(ies) designated to receive donated funds. If checked, identify the name, address, contact, and type of entities designated to receive private donated funds: The Idaho Workforce Development Council (IWDC) administered grants for investments that expand high quality child care capacity using non-CCDF funds. The grants were intended to offset start-up costs for employers providing onsite/near-site child care , encourage child care provider/employer partners to expand number of children served, and support with recruiting and training of qualified childcare staff. Childcare grant participants demonstrated private investments of at least 50% of the grant funds requested, these private investments have been recorded and verified by the Idaho Workforce Development Council (514 W Jefferson St. Ste. 131 Boise, ID 83702) which financial information provided to the lead agency in full alignment with our record retention policies for matching purposes. [ ] No. c. Does the Lead Agency certify that, if State expenditures for pre-Kindergarten programs are used to meet the MOE requirements, the following is true: • The Lead Agency did not reduce its level of effort in full-day/full-year child care services. • The Lead Agency ensures that pre-Kindergarten programs meet the needs of working parents. • The estimated percentage of the MOE requirement that will be met with pre-Kindergarten expenditures (does not to exceed 20 percent). • If the percentage is more than 10 percent of the MOE requirement, the State will coordinate its pre-Kindergarten and child care services to expand the availability of child care. Public pre-Kindergarten funds may also serve as MOE funds as long as the State can describe how it will coordinate pre-Kindergarten and child care services to expand the availability of child care while using public pre-Kindergarten funds as no more than 20 percent of the State's MOE or 30 percent of its matching funds in a single fiscal year. If expenditures for pre-Kindergarten services are used to meet the MOE requirement, does the Lead Agency certify that the State or Territory has not reduced its level of effort in full-day/full-year child care services? [x] Yes. [ ] No. If no, describe:
heading: 8.2 Optional Use of Combined Funds, CCDF Matching, and Maintenance-of-Effort Funds
