body: Lead Agencies may use CCDF funds to establish or support a system or network of local or regional child care resource and referral (CCR&R) organizations that is coordinated, to the extent determined by the Lead Agency, by a statewide public or private non-profit, community-based or regionally based, lead child care resource and referral organization (such as a statewide CCR&R network). If Lead Agencies use CCDF funds for local CCR&R organizations, the local or regional CCR&R organizations supported by those funds must, at the direction of the Lead Agency: • Provide parents in the State with consumer education information concerning the full range of child care options (including faith-based and community-based child care providers), analyzed by provider, including child care provided during non-traditional hours and through emergency child care centers, in their area. • To the extent practicable, work directly with families who receive assistance to offer the families support and assistance to make an informed decision about which child care providers they will use to ensure that the families are enrolling their children in the most appropriate child care setting that suits their needs and one that is of high quality (as determined by the Lead Agency). • Collect data and provide information on the coordination of services and supports, including services under Part B, Section 619 and Part C of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. • Collect data and provide information on the supply of and demand for child care services in areas of the State and submit the information to the Lead Agency. • Work to establish partnerships with public agencies and private entities, including faith- based and community-based child care providers, to increase the supply and quality of child care services in the State and, as appropriate, coordinate their activities with the activities of the Lead Agency and local agencies that administer funds made available through CCDF. 8.3.1 Funding a system or network of CCR&R organization(s) Does the Lead Agency fund a system or network of local or regional CCR&R organization(s)? [ ] No. The Lead Agency does not fund a system or network of local or regional CCR&R organization(s) and has no plans to establish one. [ ] No, but the Lead Agency has plans to develop a system or network of local or regional CCR&R organization(s). [x] Yes. The Lead Agency funds a system or network of local or regional CCR&R organization(s) with all the responsibilities outlined above. If yes, describe the activities outlined above carried out by the CCR&R organization(s), as directed by the Lead Agency: CCR&R services are provided statewide through a contract with the University of Idaho (UIdaho), which employs staff and/or contracts with other agencies to carry out the CCR&R scope of work. The scope of work for the CCR&R offices includes: (1) Working directly with families who receive child care assistance to offer the families support and assistance in making an informed decision about child care options to ensure families are enrolling their children in the most appropriate child care setting to suit their needs and that is of high quality as determined by IdahoSTARS. IdahoSTARS does this by discussing options for childcare with parents and sending resources to parents with referral information. These resources include when applicable, breastfeeding and safe sleep information, what to look for when searching for care, questions to ask providers, crying baby plan, developmental screening, act early information, keeping children safe abuse and neglect information, and guidelines for human milk storage. IdahoSTARS offers standard, customized, and enhanced referrals. (2) Collecting data and providing information on the coordination of services and supports including services provided through the Individuals with Disabilities Education Improvement Act (IDEA) for children with disabilities; (3) Collecting data from referrals though follow up surveys. When unmet needs are reported, this information gets documented in the RISE Application. (4) Engaging in services to increase the supply and quality of child care services in the state through business practice training and coaching to improve sustainability and quality; (5) working with other agencies through community events and partnerships to identify and support work around expanding childcare access and as appropriate, coordinating their activities with the activities of the lead agency and/or local agencies that administer Child Care and Development Funds (CCDF); (6) Reviewing rates and contacting a minimum of 250 providers annually whose data stands out as outliers, working with the provider to correct any discrepancies for market rate quality assurance, and encouraging and assisting providers in updating their Provider Information Report; For such contracts as UIdaho, the State monitors administrative implementation and responsibilities through the Division of Welfare's Contracts and External Resource Management (CERM) team. CERM evaluated and ensures that the standards, techniques, and criteria identified in the scope of work are consistent and timely.
heading: 8.3 Coordination with Child Care Resource and Referral Systems

body: Lead Agencies must demonstrate how they encourage partnerships among other public agencies, Tribal organizations, private entities, faith-based organizations, businesses, or organizations that promote business involvement, and/or community-based organizations to leverage existing service delivery (i.e., cooperative agreement among providers to pool resources to pay for shared fixed costs and operation) to leverage existing child care and early education service delivery systems and to increase the supply and quality of child care services for children younger than age 13. 8.4.1 Lead Agency public-private partnerships Identify and describe any public-private partnerships encouraged by the Lead Agency to leverage public and private resources to further the goals of CCDF: The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare is providing review and support of the Idaho Workforce Development Council’s administration of Child Care Expansion Grants. This funding, administered by the Workforce Development Council (WDC), is increasing the number of child care seats available to working families by targeting employers and/or child care providers willing to build new or expand existing facilities. Grant participants are developing and coordinating local business partnerships in support of the expansion of available child care services in each community. With an emphasis on high- quality care, these partnerships are homegrown, diverse opportunities meeting the unique needs of Idaho’s workforce, child care providers, and children.
heading: 8.4 Public-Private Partnerships

body: Lead Agencies must establish a Statewide Child Care Disaster Plan and demonstrate how they will address the needs of children—including the need for safe child care before, during, and after a state of emergency declared by the Governor or a major disaster or emergency (as defined by Section 102 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, 42 U.S.C. 5122)—through a Statewide Disaster Plan. 8.5.1 Statewide Disaster Plan updates a. When was the Lead Agency’s Child Care Disaster Plan most recently updated and for what reason? The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare’s Continuity of Operations Plan is reviewed and maintained on an official biennial plan review cycle, the most recent review and updates were completed December 2023. b. Please certify compliance by checking the required elements the Lead Agency includes in the current State Disaster Preparedness and Response Plan. i. The plan was developed in collaboration with the following required entities: [x] State human services agency. [x] State emergency management agency. [x] State licensing agency. [x] State health department or public health department. [x] Local and State child care resource and referral agencies. [x] State Advisory Council on Early Childhood Education and Care or similar coordinating body. ii. [x] The plan includes guidelines for the continuation of child care subsidies. iii. [x] The plan includes guidelines for the continuation of child care services. iv. [x] The plan includes procedures for the coordination of post-disaster recovery of child care services. v. The plan contains requirements for all CCDF providers (both licensed and license- exempt) to have in place: [x] Procedures for evacuation. [x] Procedures for relocation. [x] Procedures for shelter-in-place. [x] Procedures for communication and reunification with families. [x] Procedures for continuity of operations. [x] Procedures for accommodations of infants and toddlers. [x] Procedures for accommodations of children with disabilities. [x] Procedures for accommodations of children with chronic medical conditions. vi. [x] The plan contains procedures for staff and volunteer emergency preparedness training. vii. [x] The plan contains procedures for staff and volunteer practice drills. viii. If any of the above are not checked, describe: ix. If available, provide the direct URL/website link to the website where the Statewide Child Care Disaster Plan is posted: 9 Family Outreach and Consumer Education CCDF consumer education requirements facilitate parental choice in child care arrangements, support parents as child care consumers who need information to make informed choices regarding the services that best suit their family’s needs, and the delivery of resources that can support child development and well-being. Lead Agency consumer education activities must provide information for parents receiving CCDF assistance, the general public, and, when appropriate, child care providers. Lead Agencies should use targeted strategies for each group to ensure tailored consumer education information and take steps to ensure they are effectively reaching all individuals, including those with limited English proficiency and those with disabilities. In this section, Lead Agencies address their consumer education practices, including details about their child care consumer education website, and the process for collecting and maintaining a record of parental complaints.
heading: 8.5 Disaster Preparedness and Response Plan

body: Lead Agencies must maintain a record of substantiated parental complaints against child care providers and make information regarding such complaints available to the public on request. Lead Agencies must also provide a detailed description of the hotline or similar reporting process for parents to submit complaints about child care providers; the process for substantiating complaints; the manner in which the Lead Agency maintains a record of substantiated parental complaints; and ways that the Lead Agency makes information on such parental complaints available to the public on request. Lead Agencies are not required to limit the complaint process to parents. 9.1.1 Parental complaint process a. Describe the Lead Agency’s hotline or similar reporting process through which parents can submit complaints about child care providers, including a link if it is a Web-based process: Parents, families, and concerned community members can submit child care complaints via email (careline@dhw.idaho.gov), fax (208-334-5531), or telephone by contacting 2-1-1 Idaho CareLine (1-800-926-2588). An online complaint form is available at the following web address: https://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/services- programs/children-families/file-child-care-complaint b. Describe how the parental complaint process ensures broad access to services for families that speak languages other than English: Language assistance services are available pre request for families that speak languages other than English. c. Describe how the parental complaint process ensures broad access to services for persons with disabilities: The Idaho CareLine (211) phone line offers a Telecommunications Device for the Deaf (TDD) phone line and accepts text messages. Complaints can also be made in writing, by fax, or electronically. d. For complaints about providers, including CCDF providers and non-CCDF providers, does the Lead Agency have a process and timeline for screening, substantiating, and responding to complaints, including information about whether the process includes monitoring? [x] Yes. If yes, describe: The complaint process is the same for all child care providers in Idaho. Parents, families, and concerned community members can submit child care complaints via email(careline@dhw.idaho.gov), fax (208-334-5531), or telephone by contacting 2-1-1 IdahoCareLine (1-800-926- 2588). Once received, the complaints are entered into a single database called the Idaho Child Care Incident Tracker. Every complaint is reviewed by the state Child Care Program specialist or the State Daycare Licensing specialist to determine the correct resources and agencies for referral. Complaints involving health and safety violations, the operation of a facility without a required license, and ratio/supervision violations may all result in an unannounced health and safety inspection. Complaints related to business practices, professionalism, billing, toilet training, meals, and activities are referred to voluntary consultation through the Child Care Resource Center. Allegations of fraud are forwarded to an Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (DHW)’s Integrity Unit that specializes in the review of child care facilities. Any complaint alleging any type of abuse or illegal activity is forwarded to local law enforcement agencies, and a follow up report is requested from the responding agency within 30 days. [ ] No. e. For substantiated parental complaints, who maintains the record for CCDF and non-CCDF providers? Records of substantiated complaints against licensed and/or providers participating with the Idaho Child Care Program and all supporting documentation are maintained indefinitely in the Idaho Child Care Concern Tracker, and summaries of substantiated complaints are published for three years on IdahoChildCareCheck.org. f. Describe how information about substantiated parental complaints is made available to the public; this information can include the consumer education website discussed in subsection 9.2: Summaries of all substantiated complaints, and the response to each complaint, are published for three years on IdahoChildCareCheck.org.
heading: 9.1 Parental Complaint Process

The website must: • Include information to assist families in understanding the Lead Agency’s policies and procedures, including licensing child care providers; • Include monitoring and inspection reports for each provider and, if available, the quality of each provider; • Provide the aggregate number of deaths, serious injuries, and the number of cases of substantiated child abuse that have occurred in child care settings; • Include contact information for local CCR&R organizations to help families access additional information on finding child care; and • Include information on how parents can contact the Lead Agency and other organizations to better understand the information on the website. 9.2.1 Consumer-friendly website Does the Lead Agency ensure that its consumer education website is consumer-friendly and easily accessible? i. Describe: 9.2.5 Aggregate data on serious injuries, deaths, and substantiated abuse Lead Agencies must post aggregate data on serious injuries, deaths, and substantiated cases of child abuse that have occurred in child care settings each year on the consumer education website. This aggregate data must include information about any child in the care of a provider eligible to receive CCDF, not just children receiving subsidies. This aggregate information on serious injuries and deaths must be separated by category of care (e.g., centers, family child care homes, and in-home care) and licensing status (i.e., licensed or license-exempt) for all eligible CCDF child care providers in the State/Territory. The information on instances of substantiated child abuse does not have to be organized by category of care or licensing status. Information must also include the total number of children in care by provider type and licensing status, so that families can better understand the data presented on serious injuries, deaths, and substantiated cases of abuse. a. [x] The total number of deaths of children in care by provider category and licensing status. iii. [x] The total number of substantiated instances of child abuse in child care settings. iv. Child care staff add the information into Idaho Child Care Incident Tracker, the Lead Agency is able to obtain aggregate data from the Incident Tracker system. ii. The definition of “substantiated child abuse” used by the Lead Agency for this requirement: Substantiated Incidents are investigated and determined to have occurred by Law Enforcement in the region where the incident occurred. iii. The definition of “serious injury” used by the Lead Agency for this requirement: Category for incidents regarding children that required hospitalization or a doctor’s care. This category is not used for minor injuries such as scrapes, diaper rash, or child-to-child biting. c. body: Lead Agencies must collect and disseminate information about the full range of child care services to promote parental choice to parents of children eligible for CCDF, the general public, and child care providers. 9.3.1 Information about CCDF availability and eligibility Describe how the Lead Agency shares information with eligible parents, the general public, and child care providers about the availability of child care services provided through CCDF and other programs for which the family may be eligible. The description should include, at a minimum, what is provided (e.g., written materials, the website, and direct communications) and what approaches are used to tailor information to parents, the general public, and child care providers. For Parents and the General Public- The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (DHW) utilizes videos to highlight the Idaho Child Care Program and its benefits to families, as well as how families can seek assistance; these videos are played statewide in the lobbies of each local office. IDHW provides information on income, eligible activities and other criteria needed for eligibility via websites (http://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/Children/ChildCareAssistance/tabid/292/Default.aspx ; https://www.livebetteridaho.org/), vendor booths, blogs (https://dhwblog.com/), and social media tools (https://www.facebook.com/IdahoHealthandWelfare/ and https://www.facebook.com/IdahoSTARS-252266474799407/?fref=ts) and brochures (https://publicdocuments.dhw.idaho.gov/WebLink/Browse.aspx?id=2892&dbid=0&repo=PUBL IC- DOCUMENTS&cr=1) are disseminated to community partners who serve families with children. IdahoSTARS has a family portal that provides information about the ICCP program https://idahostars.org/Families/Financial-Assistance-ICCP, with relevant links to the application. https://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/services-programs/children-families/apply-child-care- assistance Additionally, IdahoSTARS has created a fact sheet about qualifications and income guidelines that is passed out at public events and given to child care providers for distribution to families. Families applying for the Idaho Child Care Program are made aware of other assistance programs such as SNAP, TANF, and Medicaid at application and redetermination. Families and the general public may access program information for other assistance programs at the IDHW Website: https://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/ Families also have a dedicated webpage with family specific resources at https://idahostars.org/ Child Care Providers- The Lead Agency maintains a webpage specifically targeted to Child Care Providers including provider licensing and ICCP participation information here: https://healthandwelfare.idaho.gov/providers/child-care-providers/becoming-child-care-provider Additionally, child care providers also have a dedicated webpage with provider specific resources at https://idahostars.org/ Also at the IdahoSTARS webpage providers may access subsidy enrollment requirements and additional resources for providers here: https://idahostars.org/Child-Care-Providers/ICCP Providers are encouraged to work with locally operating Child Care Resource Centers as needed for any additional information. 9.3.2 Information about child care and other services available for parents Does the Lead Agency certify that it provides information described in 9.3.1 for the following required programs? • Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program. • Head Start and Early Head Start programs. • Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) • Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). • Women, Infants, and Children Program (WIC) program. • Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP). • Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP). • Programs carried out under IDEA Part B, Section 619 and Part C. [x] Yes. [ ] No. If no, describe: 9.3.3 Consumer statement for parents receiving CCDF services Lead Agencies must provide parents receiving CCDF services with a consumer statement in hard copy or electronically that contains general information about the CCDF program and specific information about the child care provider they select. Please certify if the Lead Agency provides parents receiving CCDF services a consumer statement that contains the following 8 requirements: 1. Health and safety requirements met by the provider 2. Licensing or regulatory requirements met by the provider 3. Date the provider was last inspected 4. Any history of violations of these requirements 5. Any voluntary quality standards met by the provider 6. How CCDF subsidies are designed to promote equal access 7. How to submit a complaint through the hotline 8. How to contact a local resource and referral agency or other community-based organization to receive assistance in finding and enrolling in quality child care Does the Lead Agency provide to families, either in hard copy or electronically, a consumer statement that contains the required information about the provider they have selected, including the eight required elements above? [x] Yes. [ ] No. If no, describe: 9.3.4 Informing families about best practices on child development Describe how the Lead Agency makes information available to parents, providers, and the general public on research and best practices concerning children’s development, including physical health and development, and information about successful parent and family engagement. At a minimum, the description should include what information is provided; how the information is provided; any distinct activities for sharing this information with parents, providers, the general public; and any partners in providing this information. For Parents • Referral and Support: Parents seeking child care referrals and information on child development can connect with a Child Care Health Consultant or Quality Consultant. These professionals offer resources and guidance on research and best practices. • Online Resources: Parents have access to the IdahoSTARS website, which provides a wealth of information and connections to local organizations catering to children birth to school age. • Parent Education: Our goal is to expand our current work to be more inclusive of families. Hosting or supporting providers in hosting parent education events focusing on topics like developmental screening and monitoring. These events aim to educate and empower parents as experts of their children and support education on key aspects of children’s development. These events can be hosted at the local child care or through virtual events in connection with Developmental Screening using the ASQ 3 and ASQ SE 2. For Providers • Training Opportunities: Providers can participate in training, sessions focused on child development, physical health and development and other domains and subcategories through the online training system housed in our RISE Application, live training sessions, or virtual options. • Coaching and Technical Assistance: Coaching and additional technical assistance is available in these categories which offers providers individualized or group coaching and training tied to specific goals of the provider. Coaching and Technical Assistance is provided on-site or virtual. • Local Resources: Providers can access lending library resources from their local Child Care Resource and Referral (CCR&R) offices located regionally. The CCR&R offices also provide flyers, brochures, and handouts with valuable information tailored to specific communities served by each region. These resources are provided in home language as much as possible. • Quality Consultants coach providers in the domains of child development, health safety and wellness, and partnerships with families and communities For General Public • Website Resources: The Parent Page of the IdahoSTARS website offer a range of family health and wellness resources. This includes general information aimed at promoting healthy environments at home and in child care settings. 9.3.5 Unlimited parental access to their children Does the Lead Agency have procedures to ensure that parents have unlimited access to their children whenever their children are in the care of a provider who receives CCDF funds: [x] Yes. [ ] No. If no, describe: 9.3.6 Informing families about best practices in social and emotional health Describe how the Lead Agency shares information with families, providers, and the general public regarding the social-emotional and behavioral and mental health of young children, including positive behavioral intervention and support models based on research and best practices for those from birth to school age: Parents Parents who contact the Child Care Resource and Referral office (CCR&R) seeking a referral for child care and who request information on children’s mental health may be connected with their child care health consultant who can provide contacts for additional information and resources pertaining to local providers and organizations focusing on children’s mental health. Parents may also access the IdahoSTARS Facebook page and the IdahoSTARS website for additional resources. Parents who contact their CCR&R may also receive information through flyers, brochures, and other handouts contained in the CCR&R resource packets. Resource packets are specific to the local communities and covers birth to school-age children. Parents at programs in the Idaho Pyramid Collaborative At every tier of the Pyramid Model, programs and child care providers consider what strategies might be used to welcome and support diverse families, how to create opportunities to learn from families, strategies for partnering with families to promote child outcomes, and provide supports and services that families might need to promote their child’s development. These strategies are evaluated using the program level Benchmarks of Quality which provides each program with key components to incorporate into their program level and classroom level ways to meet implementation fidelity. Some strategies are providing information directly to families on how to build strong relationships, teaching social and emotional skills as home, using the National Center for Pyramid Model Innovation (NCPMI) resources (The Backpack Series, Making Life Easier, Social Stories, Family Articles), asking parents for input into Program Wide Expectations, and partnering with families on classroom specific initiatives. Providers Training opportunities are available through IdahoSTARS to providers who seek to gain information on early childhood mental health. Idaho’s QRIS, Steps to Quality, has embedded essential training which includes specific content on this topic area, and additional lending library resources are available from their local CCR&Rs. IdahoSTARS is a lead partner of the Idaho Pyramid Model Collaborative State Team working to implement positive behavioral intervention and supports to Idaho early childhood programs through the Pyramid Model framework. The Idaho Pyramid Model Collaborative provides training, coaching, and technical assistance supports to child care programs, Head Start programs, and school district IDEA Part B, Section 619 programs. Programs enrolled in the collaborative have access to over 18 hours of Live or self-paced online training on implementation of Pyramid Model practices which include Nurturing and Responsive Environments, High Quality Environments, Teaching Social and Emotional Skills, Teaching Problem Solving, Teaching Friendship Skills, and Tier 3 interventions (Prevent Teach Reinforce) for children exhibiting persistent challenging behavior in their first year. The second year of the road map includes training, coaching, and technical assistance including training on implicit bias and individualized supports(visual supports, peer mediated skills.) The final year on the Idaho Pyramid Model Professional Development road map, includes coaching, training , and technical assistance on trauma informed care and diversity, equity, inclusion topics, and provider wellness. At the Program level, program leaders and their leadership teams attend monthly program calls with IdahoSTARS to support the development of Systems, policies, and procedures to support the implementation fidelity of Pyramid Model practices in their programs including policies and procedures on how to respond to challenging behavior and suspension, expulsion, and exclusion. A statewide network of Pyramid Model coaches, which include IdahoSTARS Quality Consultants, are supported by a state program coach trained in behavioral intervention and support. Program practices are evaluated using the Teach Pyramid Observation Tool (TPOT) for Preschool classrooms, the Teaching Pyramid Infant and Toddler Observation Tool (TPITOS), which guides program coaching plans and assists in progress monitoring. Programs practices are evaluated using the Benchmarks of Quality (BoQ). Providers can also become specialized in infant/toddler mental health through enhanced credentials. • Child care Health Consultants are available statewide to assist providers with addressing questions/concerns that focus on early childhood mental health. General public The Parent pages of the IdahoSTARS website contains information on ￿Aim Early Idaho￿ (www.aimearlyidaho.org) and on children with disabilities. The Provider pages includes the child care health consultant information with links to early childhood mental health. The IdahoSTARS Facebook contains posts with resources and information on early childhood mental health. CCR&R staff participate in community events and disseminate information/resources using brochures, flyers, and/or handouts. 9.3.7 Policies on the prevention of the suspension and expulsion of children a. The Lead Agency must have policies to prevent the suspension and expulsion of children from birth to age 5 in child care and other early childhood programs receiving CCDF funds. Describe those policies and how those policies are shared with families, providers, and the general public: IdahoSTARS does promote education and training to child care providers on addressing and understanding challenging behaviors and has professional development opportunities as an option for providers inclusive of training and targeted technical assistance (TTA) on challenging behavior and implicit bias. Providers can engage in general training, coaching, and targeted technical assistance (TTA) on addressing and preventing challenging behavior, implicit bias, and developing social emotional competencies in children. Providers engaged in the Idaho Pyramid Collaborative that serve these populations will have enhanced training, coaching, and technical assistance that extends beyond classroom practices that support understanding of nurturing and responsive relationships with children, families, and co-workers, universal practices that support high quality environments, social and emotional competencies, and individualized supports for children with persistent challenging behaviors. The Framework also addresses program systems, policies, and procedures to explicitly address implicit bias, implement culturally responsive practices, use data systems to understand potential discipline equity issues and develop policies and procedures around challenging behavior and suspension and expulsion. IdahoSTARS also promotes and provides families with an outline of Steps to Choosing Safe and Healthy Child Care which encompasses 3 steps - Look, Check, Ask - pertaining to finding quality child care to meet their child’s needs. A child care checklist, in both English and Spanish, is available and promoted when conducting child care referrals to parents, including which questions to ask when conducting interviews with child care providers. This checklist includes how to ask about and request documents that support positive, clear, consistent guidance practices. b. Describe what policies, if any, the Lead Agency has to prevent the suspension and expulsion of school-age children from child or youth care settings receiving CCDF funds: Providers that engage with IdahoSTARS and serve school-age children have access to training, coaching, and targeted technical assistance in addressing and preventing challenging behavior, implicit bias, and social emotional competencies. Providers engaged in the Idaho Pyramid Collaborative that serve these populations will have enhanced training, coaching, and technical assistance that extends beyond classroom practices that support understanding of nurturing and responsive relationships with children, families, and co-workers, universal practices that support high quality environments, social and emotional competencies, and individualized supports for children with persistent challenging behaviors. The Framework also addresses program systems, policies, and procedures to explicitly address implicit bias, implement culturally responsive practices, use data systems to understand potential discipline equity issues and develop policies and procedures around challenging behavior and suspension and expulsion.

body: Lead Agencies must provide information on developmental screenings to parents as part of the intake process for families participating in CCDF and to child care providers through training and education. This information must include: • Existing resources and services that the State can make available in conducting developmental screenings and providing referrals to services when appropriate for children who receive child care assistance, including the coordinated use of the Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnosis, and Treatment program under the Medicaid program carried out under Title XIX of the Social Security Act and developmental screening services available under IDEA Part B, Section 619 and Part C; and, • A description of how a family or child care provider can use these resources and services to obtain developmental screenings for children who receive subsidies and who might be at risk of cognitive or other developmental delays, which can include social, emotional, physical, or linguistic delays. Information on developmental screenings, as in other consumer education information, must be accessible for individuals with limited English proficiency and individuals with disabilities. 9.4.1 Developmental screenings Does the Lead Agency collect and disseminate information on the following: a. Existing resources and services available for obtaining developmental screening for parents receiving CCDF, the general public, and child care providers. [x] Yes. [ ] No. If no, describe: b. Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnosis, and Treatment program under the Medicaid program—carried out under Title XIX of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1396 et seq.)— and developmental screening services available under Part B, Section 619 and Part C of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (20 U.S.C. 1419, 1431 et seq.). [x] Yes. [ ] No. If no, describe: c. Developmental screenings to parents receiving a subsidy as part of the intake process. [x] Yes. If yes, include the information provided, ways it is provided, and any partners in this work: All notices related to ICCP eligibility and participation include information for parents related to resources for accessing developmental screenings through partnered programs at IDHW. Child Care Providers are introduced to developmental screenings through the ICCP in Office Orientation as they decide to become an ICCP provider. IdahoSTARS has embedded an emerging indicator in our state quality and rating improvement system inclusive of the use of developmental monitoring and screening. Child care providers engaged with the Idaho Pyramid Model Collaborative begin using developmental screeners as a component of their roadmap in Year 2 or Year 3 of our three year roadmap. Providers additionally have access to training and Targeted Technical Assistance (TTA) associated with developmental screeners specifically the ASQ 3 and ASQ SE 2. General information on developmental screening is located on the IdahoSTARS website in the Basics of Child Development tab. [ ] No. If no, describe: d. How families receiving CCDF services or child care providers receiving CCDF can use the available resources and services to obtain developmental screenings for children at risk for cognitive or other developmental delays. [x] Yes. [ ] No. If no, describe: 10 Program Integrity and Accountability Program integrity and accountability activities are integral to the effective administration of the CCDF program. As stewards of federal funds, Lead Agencies must ensure strong and effective internal controls to prevent fraud and maintain continuity of services to meet the needs of children and families. In order to operate and maintain a strong CCDF program, regular evaluation of the program’s internal controls as well as comprehensive training for all entities involved in the administration of the program are imperative. In this section, Lead Agencies will describe their internal controls and how those internal controls effectively ensure integrity and accountability. These accountability measures should address reducing fraud, waste, and abuse, including program violations and administrative errors and should apply to all CCDF funds.

body: Lead Agencies must ensure the integrity of the use of CCDF funds through effective fiscal management and must ensure that financial practices are in place. Lead Agencies must have effective fiscal management practices in place for all CCDF expenditures. 10.1.1 Organizational structure to support integrity and internal controls Describe how the Lead Agency’s organizational structure ensures the oversight and implementation of effective internal controls that promote and support program integrity and accountability. Describe: 1. Assignment of authority and responsibilities related to program integrity In Idaho, the CCDF Program is administered by the CCDF Administrator known locally as the Child Care Program Manager. CCDF is administered within the Division of Self Reliance as part of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (IDHW). Within IDHW, the CCDF administrator works with other divisions, bureaus, and programs to ensure the program is ran with effective internal controls with specific attention to program integrity. IDHW’s organizational structure is designed to ensure rigorous oversight and implementation of internal controls that bolster program integrity and accountability. 2. and 3. Delegation of duties and coordination of activities Duties are delegated to staff based on their job title and essential job functions. Staff are trained on items such as Confidentiality, Program Integrity, HIPAA policies, grant administration and security training to ensure and promote program integrity. The CCDF administrator meets routinely and as needed with the managers supervising and the staff maintaining the following efforts: Self Reliance Operations- overseeing the Customer Support Staff and Self Reliance Specialists conducting subsidy eligibility determinations. Self Reliance Integrity Unit- The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare’s Division of Welfare houses a program integrity unit. The Self-Reliance Integrity Unit (SRIU) staff are responsible for program integrity and completion of all aspects of case work. They review programs including Medicaid, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, Idaho Child Care Program, Temporary Assistance in Idaho, and Aid to the Aged, Blind and Disabled. They must review of all facets of casework to include interviewing, data collection, fact gathering, case set up, error detection, case correction, processing eligibility, processing overpayments, review all actions for intent to receive benefits without entitlement, and completion of all fraud actions. Fraud actions include completing intentional program violations, hearings, overpayments, and preparing cases for prosecution. All actions must align to state and federal guidelines. Self Reliance Resolutions Unit- managing client and provider overpayments, fair hearings and appeals, escalations, and public records requests. Bureau of Compliance and Support including CERM (Contracts and External Resource Management) Team- This team monitors administrative implementation and responsibilities and ensures that the standards, techniques, and criteria identified in the contract’s scope of work are consistent and timely. This team also reviews and processes the division’s invoices. Division of Management Services- provides administrative services to support the department. The division oversees units such as facilities, criminal history background checks, internal audit, and investigation services. Division of Financial Services- ensures adequate cash is available for the department to meet its financial obligations and functions as the financial liaison to human services programs by drawing federal funds from the U S Treasury to meet immediate cash needs of federally funded programs; Requesting state general and dedicated funds through the Office of the State Controller; Preparing expenditure reports; Preparing and submitting the department's annual budget request to the Division of Financial Management and Legislative Services; Distributing appropriated funding to operating budgets within the department; Monitoring program expenditure trends to allocated funding; Preparing various financial analysis and reporting for division and executive management; Monitoring established positions; Researching and compiling historical expenditure and revenue information. 4. Communication between fiscal and program staff. All invoices are reviewed for allowable uses and contract compliance prior to payment. Program and Fiscal staff meet each month to review expenditures and monitor budgets. The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare's finance department tracks expenditures to specific accounts and funding sources. Monthly reports are provided to divisions for review as well as quarterly budget meetings take place to review budgets. 5. Segregation of duties. All contracted entities submit monthly expenditures for which the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare's Contracts and External Resource Management (CERM) reviews for accuracy and then submits to the fiscal department for processing, approval, and payment. Contract monitoring tools are developed in coordination with the program, but monitoring is conducted independently by CERM team staff. Findings are submitted to the Child Care Program Manager for review and approval prior to submission to the contractor. If any items were found deficient, the monitor team meets with the contract manager to discuss possible adverse conditions and determine the severity of each. Developing and organizing deficiencies is critical to the process. It will assist in determining whether all pertinent information was obtained during the monitor and facilitate discussions and decisions related to the potential findings. Each finding is supported with specific examples and concrete details. The CERM team submits final results to contractor, contract manager, Division of Welfare administrator, and bureau chief over Compliance and Support. If there were findings, the contractor will be given a date by which to submit reimbursement, performance improvement, or corrective action plan. 6. Establishment of checks and balances to identify potential fraud risks. Our review process is set up to find any areas in which our performance is at risk, pinpoint the area of concern (whether policy, process, or training), and quickly respond to the field needs either at the local level or roll out statewide based on the findings. For each processing center/field office reviewed, the case reviews incorporate initial contact with the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare through approval/denial as well as acting on changes. We review program access, integrity, system keying standards, and maintenance. Our reviews also include customer service standards and timeliness. Our review profile captures error causes and we have reports which help us to identify any error trends. Any errors discovered are sent for immediate correction. Errors are shared with the field program managers for individual performance management as well as used for identifying statewide trends. The bureau chiefs for operations and operations design identify areas in which we can provide statewide training when necessary which supports our statewide business model. Include the following elements in your description: 1. Assignment of authority and responsibilities related to program integrity. 2. Delegation of duties. 3. Coordination of activities. 4. Communication between fiscal and program staff. 5. Segregation of duties. 6. Establishment of checks and balances to identify potential fraud risks. 7. Other activities that support program integrity. 10.1.2 Fiscal management practices Describe how the Lead Agency ensures effective fiscal management practices for all CCDF expenditures, including: a. Fiscal oversight of CCDF funds, including grants and contracts. Describe: The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (DHW) has real time verification standards embedded into initial eligibility processes. In real time, self-reliance specialists can use our various interfaces to verify information necessary to determine eligibility and begin services. Monthly dependent care forms are submitted, outlining payment billed amounts completed in partnership with parents and signed by parents and providers, verifying the amounts articulated are verified by the parent and provider. The form is then submitted to DHW for payment. Each year, all providers sign a provider agreement for child care which outlines the requirements for participating in the program including appropriate record keeping. The Lead Agency maintains overall control of expenditures by monitoring performance- based contracts for compliance with federal regulations and the scope of work for all written contracts and agreements. This includes, but is not limited to, contracts for IdahoSTARS and the Health Districts. Contracts contain language that requires the contractor to certify that federal and state guidelines are followed. In addition to on-site record reviews conducted by the CERM team, contractors and Grantees are required to submit semi-annual performance reports on specific performance indicators. Additionally, all contracted entities submit monthly expenditures that are reviewed for accuracy, and contractual compliance prior to submission to the fiscal division for processing, approval, and payment. b. Tracking systems that ensure reasonable and allowable costs and allow for tracing of funds to a level of expenditure adequate to establish that such funds have not been used in violation of the provision of this part. Describe: The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare's finance department tracks expenditures to specific accounts and funding sources. Monthly reports are provided to divisions for review as well as quarterly budget meetings take place to review budgets. c. Processes and procedures to prepare and submit required state and federal fiscal reporting. Describe: The ACF-696 report is completed quarterly by the Grant Reporter within the Division of Financial Services using financial information compiled in our statewide financial management system, Luma, as well as the reporting amounts using the Child Care & Development Block Grant (CCDBG) Quarterly Workpapers. These workpapers are created using a report from Fiscal and are tied to Fiscal each month to ensure accuracy. The Grant Reporter tracks the match and MOE requirements based upon ACF annual requirements posted online. The Quarterly Workpapers are broken out by their sources, which are the Mandatory Fund, the Matching Fund and the Discretionary Fund, which includes TANF Transfer (Grant 1262TF). This aids the Lead Agency in meeting their multiple compliance requirements. The majority of the worksheets are pre-formulated and automated to prevent inaccurate information from being entered. The Child Care Program Manger provides secondary a review of the work papers each month and there is a double check at the bottom of the spreadsheet to confirm there are no variances. The report is then routed for review and approval to the Cash Analyst, Budget Analyst, and Financial Manager, all staff in the Division of Financial Services under the leadership of the Lead Agency's Chief Financial Officer. Review of the report includes comparing reported data to supporting records in the grant folder. The Unit Supervisor will also review prior quarter and year-to-date amounts to verify that amounts are reasonable. Documentation of the persons preparing, reviewing, and approving the ACF-696 are done by initialing and dating the routing slip. The ￿Report Electronically Filed￿ sign-off on the routing slip is not the date the report was filled; it is the date data entry was done. The Financial Executive Officer does a final review of the report to the supporting excel file CCDBG, the support in the report folder, and additional notes in the report folder, and if there are no errors noted, signs and submits the report. d. Other. Describe: 10.1.3 Effectiveness of fiscal management practices Describe how the Lead Agency knows there are effective fiscal management practices in place for all CCDF expenditures, including: a. How the Lead Agency defines effective fiscal management practices. Describe: Effective fiscal management practices involve regular monitoring, transparent accounting procedures, and adherence to federal and state guidelines to ensure proper allocation and use of CCDF funds. This includes detailed monthly reviews, rigorous expenditure tracking, and multiple controls for payouts, supported by advanced fiscal projection tools. b. How the Lead Agency measures and tracks results of their fiscal management practices. Describe: The Idaho Child Care Program measures the effectiveness of fiscal management through performance indicators such as expenditure rates, compliance with budget allocations, and audit results. Automated resources such as expenditure tracking systems and monthly financial reporting are utilized, in addition to frequent staff and leadership review of reports, and on-site monitoring of contracted partners measures and tracks indicators consistently. All audit results are reviewed at each level of leadership within the Division of Self Reliance and the Division of Management Services to develop improvements based on all results. c. How the results inform implementation. Describe: Both the Statewide Single Audit and the Internal Audit teams publish findings resulting from their audits. These findings indicate what caused the error, and each finding requires a management response in the form of a corrective action plan. Results of monitoring or auditing are shared with program staff and department leadership and used to impact staff training and organizational decisions. At the grant and program level, similar informal procedures are performed to correct issues that are discovered as part of the review process. d. Other. Describe: NA 10.1.4 Identifying risk Describe the processes the Lead Agency uses to identify risk in the CCDF program including: a. Each process used by the Lead Agency to identify risk (including entities responsible for implementing each process). Describe: For subsidy payments, Supervisory reviews are completed annually. Our review process is set up to find any areas in which our performance is at risk, pinpoint the area of concern (whether policy, process, or training), and quickly respond to the field needs either at the local level or roll out statewide based on the findings. For each processing center/field office reviewed, the case reviews incorporate initial contact with the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare through approval/denial as well as acting on changes. We review program access, integrity, system keying standards, and maintenance. Our reviews also include customer service standards and timeliness. Additionally, all eligibility staff are able to submit any subsidy case or provider for additional review by the Self Reliance Integrity Unit if concerns are identified. All contracts contain language that requires the contractor to certify that federal and state guidelines are followed. In addition to on-site record reviews conducted by the CERM team, contractors and Grantees are required to submit semi-annual performance reports on specific performance indicators. Additionally, all contracted entities submit monthly expenditures that are reviewed for accuracy, and contractual compliance prior to submission to the fiscal division for processing, approval, and payment. Contract monitoring tools are developed in coordination with the program, but monitoring is conducted independently by CERM team staff. Findings are submitted to the Child Care Program Manager for review and approval prior to submission to the contractor. If any items were found deficient, the monitor team meets with the contract manager to discuss possible adverse conditions and determine the severity of each. Any finding is supported with specific examples and concrete details. The CERM team submits final results to contractor, contract manager, Division of Welfare administrator, and bureau chief over Compliance and Support. If there were findings, the contractor is given a date by which to submit reimbursement, performance improvement, or corrective action plan. b. The frequency of each risk assessment. Describe: Risk assessment is completed on an ongoing basis. Daily evaluation occurs in eligibility determination. Ongoing supervisory quality control reviews are conducted on subsidy cases as well. A thorough risk assessment is completed prior to awarding any subgrant or contract and upon each annual renewal. All child care providers complete an updated Provider Agreement annually validating that they are not on the Office of Inspector General’s Exclusion List. The Lead Agency conducts the triennial improper payments review in addition to frequent legislative audits of all levels of programming. c. How the Lead Agency uses risk assessment results to inform program improvement. Describe: Our review profile captures error causes, and we have reports which help us to identify any error trends. Any errors discovered are sent for immediate correction. Errors are shared with the field program managers for individual performance management as well as used for identifying statewide trends. The bureau chiefs for operations and operations design identify areas in which we can provide statewide training when necessary, which supports our statewide business model. For contracts and subgrants, the Lead Agency requires risk assessments to evaluate potential subrecipients’ capacity to comply with federal and state regulations and the terms of the subaward. The aim is to identify the appropriate allocation of monitoring resources towards subrecipients based on their risk of noncompliance with Federal statutes, regulations, and the terms and conditions of specific subawards. This process is intended to optimize resource allocation, minimize waste, and enhance decision-making in the monitoring of subrecipients. Programs document assessment results and decisions regarding monitoring activities for each subrecipient. These records must be signed and dated by monitoring staff, supervisors or managers, and designated compliance officers. Clear communication of results to all relevant parties is essential to ensure understanding and alignment on planned monitoring activities. d. How the Lead Agency knows that the risk assessment processes utilized are effective. Describe: The Lead Agency requires all subgranting and contracting programs to develop a monitoring plan that covers every subrecipient. Considerations such as staffing resources and the geographic distribution of subrecipients across the State, guide the development of monitoring activities. Adequate oversight is crucial for maintaining performance standards, particularly amid staffing changes and other influencing factors. Early issue resolution can preempt problems and minimize the need for extensive technical assistance later on. The Lead Agency maintains overall control of expenditures by monitoring performance- based contracts for compliance with federal regulations and the scope of work for all written contracts and agreements. This includes, but is not limited to, contracts for IdahoSTARS and the Health Districts. Contracts contain language that requires the contractor to certify that federal and state guidelines are followed. In addition to on-site record reviews conducted by the CERM team, contractors and Grantees are required to submit semi-annual performance reports on specific performance indicators. Additionally, all contracted entities submit monthly expenditures that are reviewed for accuracy, and contractual compliance prior to submission to the fiscal division for processing, approval, and payment. The results of the submitted reports and on-site monitoring evaluation continue to demonstrate our program’s success with minimal findings, expeditious resolutions, and compliance rates exceeding the contractual requirements. The Idaho Child Care Program has received successful results in triannual error rate reviews, annual Legislative audits, and semi-annual monitoring of CCDF funded contracts indicates successful program implementation and risk management. e. Other. Describe: NA 10.1.5 Processes to train about CCDF requirements and program integrity Describe the processes the Lead Agency uses to train staff of the Lead Agency and other agencies engaged in the administration of CCDF, and child care providers about program requirements and integrity. a. Describe how the Lead Agency ensures that all staff who administer the CCDF program (including through MOUs, grants, and contracts) are informed and trained regarding program requirements and integrity. i. Describe the training provided to staff members around CCDF program requirements and program integrity: The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare's Division of Self Reliance trains all self-reliance specialists on each program administered within the division. Training includes videos on program rules, policies, general program details, process documents, helpful tools, release notices, and monthly management reviews. ii. Describe how staff training is evaluated for effectiveness: The Bureau Chief over Operations monitors various reports on a daily, weekly, and monthly basis. Program managers receive reports on their region to identify and review results and create training opportunities in areas of the business requiring additional assistance to meet targets. Monthly supervisor reviews aid in the identification and prevention of agency errors because it allows for a review of more eligibility cases and training where needed. iii. Describe how the Lead Agency uses program integrity data (e.g., error rate results, risk assessment data) to inform ongoing staff training needs: Idaho uses program integrity data to identify risk areas for training and or policy clarifications. Idaho conducts error rate reviews in real time allowing any potential errors to immediately become learning and training opportunities for staff to learn from supervisors and case reviewers. When not conducting case reviews for the error rate, staff receive regular ongoing training on any policy or rule changes made to the program and materials are updated on a regular basis using feedback from partners to improve process documents and policy guidance. b. Describe how the Lead Agency ensures all providers for children receiving CCDF funds are informed and trained regarding CCDF program requirements and program integrity: i. Describe the training for providers around CCDF program requirements and program integrity: Every provider who starts a child care business that accepts CCDF funds receives an Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) orientation with a CCRC Resource Specialist. The provider is provided slides and a provider guidebook with a follow-up visit after they have completed the process and has received a vendor number. The content of the ICCP orientation, supporting materials, and follow-up contact informs the provider of ICCP rules, required processes and support with implementing the requirements. Every new provider is introduced to their local CCRC staff, their customer support team, the 2-1-1 Idaho Careline, and the IdahoSTARS website. Local and state resources are provided and opportunities for professional development are shared and encouraged. The Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP) notifies providers of policy changes through required annually updated provider agreements, email and mailed policy notifications, IdahoSTARS newsletters, and pop-ups in the RISE database system. ii. Describe how provider training is evaluated for effectiveness: Provider training is evaluated through audit outcomes, training requests, and based on informally extracting recurrent themes in informal and formal technical assistance provided to child care providers within their regions. iii. Describe how the Lead Agency uses program integrity data (e.g., error rate results, risk assessment data) to inform ongoing provider training needs: Staff from the Self Reliance Integrity Unit and Self Reliance Fair Hearing Unit meet regularly with Child Care Program staff to review data, challenging cases, policy questions, and process needs for all child care cases. Any consistent findings associated to providers are reviewed and shared with IdahoSTARS leadership for referral for technical assistance or updated trainings. Additionally, consistent findings can be used to inform annual updates to the Provider Agreement for improved clarity and compliance. 10.1.6 Evaluate internal control activities Describe how the Lead Agency uses the following to regularly evaluate the effectiveness of Lead Agency internal control activities for all CCDF expenditures. a. Error rate review triennial report results (if applicable). Describe who this information is shared with and how the Lead Agency uses the information to evaluate the effectiveness of its internal controls: Idaho conducts error rate reviews in real time allowing any potential errors to immediately become learning and training opportunities for staff to learn from supervisors and case reviewers. ACF-404 results are shared with division leadership, child care program staff, and quality control team and Lead Agency staff may use error rate results if a pattern is identified concerning incorrect eligibility decisions and is promptly addressed through training or policy updates. Final results are shared with legislative auditors when requested and inform staff training, organizational decisions, policy development and ongoing refinements. b. Audit results. Describe who this information is shared with and how the Lead Agency uses the information to evaluate the effectiveness of its internal controls: Idaho’s Legislative Services Office conducts routine audits of IDHW programs including this Idaho Child Care Program. Audits are either fiscal or performance in nature during which state auditors review the Lead Agency’s policies, procedures, fiscal records, systems and databases, and relevant documents to determine compliance with state and federal requirements. Audits provide the Lead Agency with regular outside analysis of program operations and potential weaknesses in the system. Audit outcomes are made publicly available, presented to the legislature annually, and shared with leadership from the Divisions of Self Reliance and Management Services, and child care program staff. Lead Agency staff work to promptly address any findings through staff training, policy updates, and/or system improvements. c. Other. Describe who this information is shared with and how the Lead Agency uses the information to evaluate the effectiveness of its internal controls: NA 10.1.7 Identified weaknesses in internal controls Has the Lead Agency or other entity identified any weaknesses in its internal controls? a. [x] No. If no, describe when and how it was most recently determined that there were no weaknesses in the Lead Agency’s internal controls. The Lead Agency routinely works to improve internal controls via data management, process improvements, and consistent training. The child care program participates in annual audits conducted by Legislative Services Office, any potential findings are promptly addressed and resolved. At this time there are no concerns with internal controls. b. [ ] Yes. If yes, what were the indicators? How did you use the information to strengthen your internal controls?
heading: 10.1 Effective Internal Controls

body: Lead Agencies must have the necessary controls to identify fraud and other program violations to ensure program integrity. Program violations can include both intentional and unintentional client and/or provider violations, as defined by the Lead Agency. These violations and errors, identified through the error-rate review process and other review processes, may result in payment or nonpayment (administrative) errors and may or may not be the result of fraud, based on the Lead Agency definition. 10.2.1 Strategies used to identify and prevent program violations Check the activities the Lead Agency employs to ensure program integrity, and for each checked activity, identify what type of program violations the activity addresses, describe the activity and the results of these activities based on the most recent analysis. a. [x] Share/match data from other programs (e.g., TANF program, Child and Adult Care Food Program, Food and Nutrition Service (FNS), Medicaid) or other databases (e.g., State Directory of New Hires, Social Security Administration, Public Assistance Reporting Information System (PARIS)). i. [x] Intentional program violations. Describe the activities, the results of these activities, and how they inform better practice: Idaho currently shares data with the between the following programs: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), Aid to the Aged, Blind, and Disabled (AABD), and Medicaid as all of these programs share the same eligibility system. The sharing and matching of data with other programs helps prevent intentional program violations because it can show information that is required to be reported for the Child Care program but may have not been reported, although ICCP only acts on information from these other programs if the recipient is required to report it or if it will benefit the household. The results of this activity also reduce the risk of incorrect eligibility determinations. The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (DHW) has an integrity unit who monitors PARIS matches monthly. The report is SNAP related and used across all programs. The report reflects households who may be receiving benefits in more than one state. This information is reviewed and if an IPV has been committed, a waiver of disqualification hearing is sent to the customer. If not signed, an administrative hearing is requested. If an Intentional Program Violation (IPV) was acknowledged, the party who committed the IPV loses eligibility for ICCP and an overpayment may be processed. If fraud is detected, it is routed to a Fraud Investigator to review and determine the proper course of action. Program staff meet with staff from the Self Reliance Resolutions Unit and Self Reliance Integrity Unit to review the outcomes of data sharing and reports and routinely monitors for patterns and errors to learn about opportunities to improve processes and policies to prevent negative client or provider outcomes such as IPV’s, unintentional program violations, and agency errors. ii. [x] Unintentional program violations. Describe the activities, the results of these activities, and how they inform better practice: Idaho currently shares data with the between the following programs: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), Aid to the Aged, Blind, and Disabled (AABD), and Medicaid as all of these programs share the same eligibility system. The sharing and matching of data with other programs helps prevent unintentional program violations because it can show information that is required to be reported for the Child Care program but may have not been reported, although ICCP only acts on information from these other programs if the recipient is required to report it or if it will benefit the household. The results of this activity also reduce the risk of incorrect eligibility determinations. The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (DHW) has an integrity unit who monitors PARIS matches monthly. The report is SNAP related and used across all programs. The report reflects households who may be receiving benefits in more than one state. If an unintentional program violation is determined, an overpayment is processed. Program staff meet with staff from the Self Reliance Resolutions Unit and Self Reliance Integrity Unit to review the outcomes of data sharing and reports and routinely monitors for patterns and errors to learn about opportunities to improve processes and policies to prevent negative client or provider outcomes such as IPV’s, unintentional program violations, and agency errors. iii. [x] Agency errors. Describe the activities, the results of these activities, and how they inform better practice:: Idaho currently shares data with the between the following programs: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), Aid to the Aged, Blind, and Disabled (AABD), and Medicaid as all of these programs share the same eligibility system. Describe the activities and the results of these activities based on the most recent analysis: Intentional Program Violations (IPV) - (IDAPA: 16.06.12.702))- An IPV is an intentionally false or misleading action or statement as identified below in Subsections 702.01 through 702.08 of this rule. An IPV is established when a family member or the child care provider admits the IPV in writing and waives the right to an administrative hearing, or when determined by an administrative hearing, a court decision, or through deferred adjudication. Deferred adjudication exists when the court defers a determination of guilt because the accused family member or child care provider meets the terms of a court order or an agreement with the prosecutor. Penalties for an IPV - (IDAPA: 16.06.12.703) When the the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (DHW) determines an IPV was committed, the party who committed the IPV loses eligibility for the Idaho Child Care Program (ICCP). If an individual has committed an IPV, the entire family is ineligible for child care benefits. If a child care provider has committed an IPV, the provider is ineligible to receive payments. The period of ineligibility for each offense, for both participants and providers, is as follows: First Offense. 12 months for the first IPV or fraud offense, or the length of time specified by the court Second Offense. 24 months for the second IPV or fraud offense, or the length of time specified by the court Third Offense. Permanent ineligibility for the third or subsequent IPV or fraud offense, or the length of time specified by the court Fair Hearing Process - (Benefits Process Manual: "Fair Hearing Process") Clients have 30 days from the date of the decision to request a fair hearing. Fair Hearing Officers review and respond to all requests within five calendar days of the "fair hearing requested" task being set. They communicate the status of reinstatement/continuance of benefits pending the hearing result to the customer within five calendar days of the "fair hearing requested" task being set. Then work with the client to coordinate and manage all aspects of a fair hearing to completion. The result of client disqualification temporary or permanently prevents ongoing misuse of program funds and maintains program sustainability. ii. [x]Disqualify the provider. Describe the activities and the results of these activities based on the most recent analysis: Termination of Provider Status - (Idaho Code 56-209h) The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (DHW) may terminate the provider agreement of, or otherwise deny provider status for a period of us to five years from the date DHW's action becomes final to any individual or entity providing the Idaho Child Care Program. Provider Notification - (IDAPA 16.06.17.750) When the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (DHW) determines actions defined in Sections 701 through 705, 750, and 751 of these rules are appropriate, it will send written notice of the decision to the provider or person. The notice will state the basis for the action, the length of the action, the effect of the section on that person's ability to provide services under state and federal programs, and the person's appeal rights. Notice to State Licensing Authorities - (Benefits Process Manual: "Fair Hearing Process") DHW will promptly notify all appropriate licensing authorities having responsibility for licensing of a DHW action, and the facts and circumstances of that action. DHW may request certain actions be taken and that DHW be informed of actions taken. A certified letter serves as written notice of the decision. A decision issued by DHW in the Division of Welfare program will be final and effective unless an individual or representative files a written notice of appeal within 30 days from the date the decision was mailed. Appeals- Appeals can be sent to: Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Administrative Procedures Section (APS) P.O. Box 83720, Boise, Idaho 83720- 0036 or APS@dhw.idaho.gov (Letter of termination). Fair hearing officers review and respond to all requests within 14 calendar days of receipt of the appeal. They communicate the status of reinstatement of the provider agreement pending the hearing result to the provider, then work with the provider to coordinate and manage all aspects of a fair hearing to completion.
